note: Structured outputs of completed agents from the critique/research workflow (run wf_f11a278a-701), saved so synthesis can resume without re-running them.

findings.title: No 'source unavailable' branch for the named data feeds (Farside, funding/OI, options, Polymarket/Kalshi, Fear & Greed)
findings.issue: STEP 1 names specific sources (Farside, Polymarket/Kalshi) and asks for numbers that only live behind sites the runtime cannot fetch (ETF daily flows, funding, open interest, options max pain/skew, Fear & Greed). The only instruction for missing data is a trailing RULES line ('Say I don't know where data is missing') that is not attached to any step, has no priority order, and has no consequence for the forecast. In practice a tool-using model will (a) spend its search budget on 8 categories with roughly 20 sub-items in list order, (b) fill gaps from stale search snippets or training memory, and (c) still produce a confident STEP 4 adjustment as if flows and positioning data were present. There is also no cap on tool calls, so runtimes with a small search budget truncate silently.
findings.evidence: Harness context: Farside, Polymarket, Kalshi, alternative.me and Coinglass-type endpoints are blocked in this environment; only WebSearch works. Halawi et al. 2024 report their retrieval-augmented forecaster only nears crowd performance when it retrieves at least 5 relevant articles and does best when the crowd is uncertain (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18563), i.e. sparse retrieval should push the forecast back toward the base rate rather than toward a confident narrative.
findings.fix: Rewrite STEP 1 as a tiered checklist with an explicit budget and a NOT FOUND token. Tier A (must attempt, max 6 searches): price/24h/7d, scheduled catalysts with dates, next FOMC odds, ETF flows. Tier B (only if budget remains, max 4): funding/OI, options expiry/skew, prediction-market odds, Fear & Greed. Tier C: everything else. For every item emit one line 'item | value | source_id | published_date | status' with status in {FOUND, STALE, NOT FOUND}. If a source is unreachable or the number does not appear verbatim in a tool result, write NOT FOUND and do not estimate it. Add a coverage rule: 'If any Tier A item is NOT FOUND, or fewer than 2 Tier B items are FOUND, keep Q1 and Q2 within 45-55% and say why.' Report the count of searches used.

findings.title: 'Cite sources, note dates' is unenforceable and invites fabricated URLs and invented flow numbers
findings.issue: The prompt says 'no answers from memory; cite sources, note dates' but defines no citation format, no link between a number and its source, and no prohibition on citing pages that were never returned by a tool. ETF daily flows, liquidation totals, funding rates and Fear & Greed readings are exactly the kind of plausible-looking figures a model will reproduce from memory with a realistic-looking Farside or Coinglass URL attached. Nothing downstream (STEP 4 adjustments, the log line) distinguishes a tool-sourced number from a recalled one, so a fabricated input silently moves the probability.
findings.evidence: Anthropic's output-consistency guidance lists 'grounding answers in retrieval' and 'constraining with examples' as the levers for reliable output (https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency). Rest is reasoning only: the prompt has no mechanism that ties a quantitative claim to a tool result.
findings.fix: Add a SOURCES block that is built only from tool results: 'S1 | URL exactly as returned by the tool | page publication date | retrieved T0'. Then: 'Every number in this response must be followed by [S#]. A number without [S#] must be labeled (unsourced estimate) and may not be used in STEP 4. Never write a URL that did not appear in a tool result this session. Never report ETF flows, funding, OI, liquidations or Fear & Greed from memory; if not in a tool result, write NOT FOUND.' Put this rule at the top of STEP 1, not in the trailing RULES block.

findings.title: Output is not machine-parseable: the log line is ambiguous and the format is prose-first
findings.issue: STEP 5 asks for 'date | price | Q1 | Q2 | Q3' but Q3 is three numbers, the date format and time zone are unspecified, 'price' has no source or timestamp, and Q1/Q2 are requested as the string 'P(up) = X%'. The line is preceded by four free-text bullets, so a scoring script has to regex a moving target. There is no example of the final block, no prompt-version tag, and no delimiter that tells a program where the parseable part starts.
findings.evidence: Anthropic's XML-tags guidance cites parseability of the response as a reason to wrap output in named tags (https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/use-xml-tags), and recommends structured outputs when a schema must be guaranteed (https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs).
findings.fix: Replace the log line with a mandatory final block: '<forecast_json>' containing one JSON object with fixed keys: prompt_version, run_id, t0_utc (ISO 8601 with Z), p0_usd, p0_source, p0_candle_close_utc, q1_p_up (0-1), q2_p_up (0-1), q3 {up_gt_4: , within_4: , down_lt_4: } summing to 1.00 within 0.005, range_7d_80pct {low, high}, coverage {tier_a_found: n/4, tier_b_found: n/4}, market_cross_check {source, implied_p_up, delta_pts or null}, flip_observation (string), holder_action (enum), sources [ {id, url, published} ]. Probabilities as decimals, not percent strings. Include one fully filled example in the prompt. Instruct: 'Nothing may follow the closing tag.' The prose sections stay above it.

findings.title: Resolution criteria are under-specified, so the Brier log cannot actually be scored
findings.issue: 'Higher than the current price 48 hours from now' has no defined t0 (prompt start? price-quote time? end of run?), 'Coinbase BTC-USD spot' does not say last trade, 1-minute close or hourly close, 'higher' is not defined as strict, and the Q3 boundaries (is exactly +4.00% in the up bucket or the middle bucket?) are undefined. A one-minute mismatch between forecaster and resolver at $77k can flip Q1 on a 0.1% move, which is inside normal noise, so the resulting Brier scores would measure clock drift rather than skill.
findings.evidence: Coinbase Exchange public candles endpoint: granularity in {60, 300, 900, 3600, 21600, 86400} seconds, max 300 candles per request, candle schema [time, low, high, open, close, volume] with time as the bucket start in UTC epoch seconds (https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/api-reference/exchange-api/rest-api/products/get-product-candles). That gives an unambiguous, no-auth resolution source the prompt does not currently pin down.
findings.fix: Add a RESOLUTION section: 't0 = the UTC timestamp of the price quote you used, written in the JSON. p0 = the close of the last completed 1-hour Coinbase Exchange BTC-USD candle at or before t0 (state its bucket start). Q1 resolves YES if the close of the 1-hour candle whose bucket starts at t0 + 48h is strictly greater than p0; Q2 uses t0 + 168h. Q3: move = close/p0 - 1; move >= +0.04 is the up bucket, move <= -0.04 is the down bucket, otherwise the middle. The scoring script pulls both closes from GET /products/BTC-USD/candles?granularity=3600.' Also state that if the model cannot obtain a price within 2 hours of t0 it must mark p0 as STALE and the run as unscoreable.

findings.title: Step order contradicts the stated design basis: search comes before the base rate, and the base rate is an unsourced anchor inside the prompt
findings.issue: The header says 'base rates first' but STEP 2 (outside view) runs after an 8-item news search, so the model forms its narrative before stating the reference class and anchors on whatever the search surfaced. The base rate itself ('~51-53%') is asserted in the prompt with no source and no volatility figure, so it functions as an anchor the model cannot verify and will echo back as if it had computed it. The 7-day standard deviation, which drives Q3, is left for the model to recall.
findings.evidence: The superforecasting prompt in Schoenegger, Park, Karger and Tetlock 2024 instructs the assistant to begin by identifying reference classes and grounding initial estimates in their base rates, then adjust on current information (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07862); the reviewed prompt reverses that order in its executable steps.
findings.fix: Swap STEP 1 and STEP 2 and make the base rate an input, not a recollection. Add an <inputs> block the user's Python fills from Coinbase daily candles each run: p_up_2d_1y, p_up_7d_1y, p_up_7d_4y, sd_7d_pct_1y, p_abs7d_gt_4pct_1y, realized_vol_30d_annualized. Instruct: 'Before any search, write your prior for Q1, Q2 and Q3 using only the <inputs> table. Searches in the next step may move each probability by at most 10 points from this prior unless you cite [S#] evidence you rate as un-priced.' Delete the hard-coded '~51-53%'.

findings.title: No handling of 'now', time zones or source staleness
findings.issue: The prompt never tells the model what time it is, what time zone dates are in, or how old a source may be before it is unusable. Search results routinely surface pages 1-7 days old; ETF flow figures are reported T+1; a 'current price' pulled from a three-day-old article is presented with the same confidence as a live quote. Catalyst times ('FOMC 2pm') are ambiguous without a zone, and '48 hours from now' has no anchor for a run that spans several minutes of tool calls.
findings.evidence: reasoning only
findings.fix: Inject 'T0_UTC = <ISO timestamp>' and 'USER_TZ = America/Chicago' (or the user's zone) as the first lines of the prompt. Add: 'Every fact carries its publication date. Freshness limits: price <= 2h old, flows/funding/OI/options <= 36h, macro/catalyst <= 7d. Anything older is STALE and may be mentioned but not used as current. All catalyst times in UTC with the USER_TZ conversion in parentheses. If T0 is missing, take it from the newest tool-result timestamp and say so in the JSON.'

findings.title: RULES contain contradictions and an unscoped probability band, so they will be violated on every run
findings.issue: (a) 'Probabilities outside 35-65% require unusually strong evidence' is not scoped to Q1/Q2. Applied to Q3 it is impossible to satisfy: with 30-day realized volatility near 47% annualized, the 7-day standard deviation is about 6.5%, giving roughly 27% per tail and 46% for the middle bucket; at the 23% low end seen in 2025-26 the middle bucket is near 79%. (b) 'No price targets without probabilities' conflicts with STEP 5's 'Key levels' and 'Expected 7-day range' bullets, which are price levels. (c) 'Move toward market odds if you differ by >10 points' has no branch for the common case where no market odds were found. (d) A hard band toward 50% risks institutionalizing the hedging bias that recent work found in LLM forecasters.
findings.evidence: BTC 30-day annualized realized volatility was 47.25% on 2026-09-07 with a 2025-26 range of about 23-45% (https://www.theblock.co/data/crypto-markets/prices/annualized-btc-volatility-30d, via WebSearch summary); the 7-day sd and bucket probabilities are my arithmetic from that figure. AIA Forecaster (Bridgewater AIA Labs, 2025) reports LLM forecasters hedge too much and that simple extremization improves scores (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07678).
findings.fix: Rewrite RULES as scoped, checkable statements: 'R1: Q1 and Q2 must lie in 0.35-0.65 unless at least two [S#]-cited un-priced items are listed in STEP 3. R2: Q3 has no band; it must be consistent with sd_7d_pct from <inputs> (state the implied probabilities first). R3: Key levels are conditional triggers, each written as level + what it would change (e.g. close above X for 2 days raises Q2 to Y); no standalone targets. R4: If no options-implied or prediction-market odds were FOUND, write market_cross_check.delta_pts = null and skip the >10-point rule.' Append a SELF-AUDIT block: one yes/no line per rule, filled before the JSON; a NO must be explained.

findings.title: Persona claim, holder-advice bullet and missing example leave the least-constrained part of the output to improvisation
findings.issue: 'You are a superforecaster with a strong track record' has no measured effect on factual accuracy and can bias toward confident tone. The bullet 'what this means for a long-term holder deciding on staged adds' has no inputs (position size, cash available, add size, decision thresholds), so each week the model invents a different framing, which is both unscoreable and the part most likely to drift into unhedged buy/sell advice. There is no worked example of the final output, so format compliance depends on the model's guess.
findings.evidence: Zheng et al., EMNLP Findings 2024, found that adding personas to system prompts does not improve performance across 162 roles and 4 model families, with gains that were small and inconsistent (https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.888/). Rest is reasoning only.
findings.fix: Keep the behavioral instructions (calibration, Brier, no edge claims) and drop the track-record persona. Add to <inputs>: position_usd, dry_powder_usd, max_add_per_week_usd, max_trim_per_week_pct, and a user-approved mapping such as 'holder_action = ADD if q2_p_up >= 0.58 and q3.down_lt_4 <= 0.25; TRIM if q2_p_up <= 0.42 and q3.up_gt_4 <= 0.25; else HOLD' (thresholds are placeholders for the user to set). Require the model to apply the mapping mechanically and put the result in holder_action, with one sentence of rationale. Include one abbreviated but complete example of the STEP 5 output and JSON block in the prompt.

critic:prompt-engineering.overall: The prompt's forecasting logic is sound and faithfully reflects the research it cites, but as an executable instruction for a tool-using agent it is under-specified exactly where failures are costly: it names data feeds the runtime cannot reach without saying what to do when they fail, it never forces a number to trace back to a tool result, and its log line cannot be parsed or resolved unambiguously, so the Brier scores it promises cannot be computed. Its own steps contradict its design basis (search before base rate) and its RULES are unscoped or self-conflicting (a 35-65% band that Q3 must violate every week, 'no targets' beside a key-levels bullet), so a compliant model will break them silently on every run. A v2 with tiered searches plus NOT FOUND handling, source-tagged numbers, an injected T0 and base-rate table, explicit candle-based resolution rules, and a fixed JSON block with an example would make it scoreable and safe to automate weekly.

findings.title: Questions are not resolvable as written: 'current price' has no timestamp, source instant, candle, time zone or tie rule
findings.issue: Q1/Q2 say 'higher than the current price' but the prompt never fixes what 'current' means. In practice the model's 'current price' is whatever a web search returns, which can be hours or days stale and from any venue. Resolution is 'Coinbase BTC-USD spot' with no instant (48h from when?), no candle convention (last trade vs 1-minute close vs 60-second average), no time zone, and no tie rule. An unresolvable question cannot be Brier-scored, which defeats the prompt's own logging step. The stale-price problem is not hypothetical: the harness context reports BTC at roughly $77-78k from mid-September search results, while the Bitstamp minute feed prints $81,102 at 15:01 UTC on 2026-09-19. A ~4-5% gap between 'search price' and live price is larger than the entire ±4% bucket width in Q3, so a stale anchor can silently flip the Q3 outcome.
findings.evidence: Live data: https://github.com/ff137/bitstamp-btcusd-minute-data (data/updates file, last row 2026-09-19 15:01 UTC, close 81,102.01). Resolution conventions used by real markets: Polymarket daily 'Bitcoin Up or Down' resolves on the Binance BTC/USDT 1-minute candle close at 12:00 PM ET vs the prior day's same candle, exact tie = 50-50 (https://polymarket.com/event/bitcoin-up-or-down-on-september-16-2026); Kalshi settles every BTC contract on a 60-second average of the CF Benchmarks BRTI (https://help.kalshi.com/en/articles/13823838-crypto-markets, https://predictionmarketspicks.com/articles/how-kalshi-settles-bitcoin).
findings.fix: Make the anchor an INPUT, not a search result: the local script (or the user) pastes 'ANCHOR: Coinbase BTC-USD 1-min candle close at <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC> = $X' at the top of the prompt. Define resolution verbatim: 'Q1 resolves YES iff the Coinbase BTC-USD 1-minute candle close at anchor+48h00m UTC is strictly greater than the anchor; equal or lower = NO. Q2 same at anchor+168h. If Coinbase data is unavailable for that minute, use the Kraken XBT/USD 1-minute close at the same instant.' Log the anchor timestamp and the resolution timestamp, and have the script fetch and write the resolution price automatically.

findings.title: The scoring loop cannot deliver a verdict at weekly cadence: hundreds to thousands of forecasts are needed to separate real skill from a coin flip
findings.issue: The prompt logs 'date | price | Q1 | Q2 | Q3' so forecasts 'can be scored later', but at one forecast per week the log is statistically inert for the realistic skill levels the prompt itself allows (35-65%). Computed: a perfectly calibrated forecaster whose true P(up) is 58% has expected Brier 0.2436 vs 0.25 for a constant 50%; the per-forecast Brier s.d. is 0.079, so the 95% CI excludes 0.25 only after ~585 forecasts (11.2 years weekly, 1.6 years daily). At 55% true skill it is ~1,520 forecasts (29 years weekly). Meanwhile the 80% interval, which is the most information-dense thing the prompt elicits and the quickest calibration check (a 52-forecast coverage test has SE ~5.5 points), is not logged at all, and Q3's three ordered buckets have no named scoring rule (Brier on buckets ignores ordering).
findings.evidence: reasoning only (power computation in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-crushpaper/726f4765-ef02-5a68-a568-426e246fec70/scratchpad/analyze.py: N = (1.96*sd/(0.25-E[Brier]))^2). Human-vs-LLM benchmark context: ForecastBench found expert forecasters beat the top LLM (p<0.001) on ~1,000 questions, i.e., large N is the norm for such comparisons (https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.19839).
findings.fix: (1) Run Q1 (48h) daily from the local script even if the human only reads the weekly digest; 365/yr is the minimum that makes a skill test feasible inside two years. (2) Extend the log line to: anchor_ts_utc | anchor_price | Q1 | Q2 | Q3(3 probs) | range80_low | range80_high | market_implied_P(up) | prompt_version | model. (3) Pre-register scoring: Brier for Q1/Q2, Ranked Probability Score for Q3, coverage + Winkler score for the 80% range, and Brier SKILL scores against three baselines (constant 50%, trailing-2y base rate, market-implied). (4) Pre-register a stopping rule: after 200 Q1 forecasts, if skill vs the market baseline is not positive, drop directional questions from the weekly check-in and keep only the rules-based holder guidance.

findings.title: Base rate is hard-coded ('~51-53%') rather than computed, and it is window-dependent: 46% to 54% depending on lookback
findings.issue: Step 2 tells the model the answer ('~51-53%') instead of asking it to derive one, which is an anchor baked into the instrument and will be echoed as if computed. The number is also only right for one window. From Bitstamp daily UTC closes: 7-day up-frequency is 54.4% (2013-2026), 53.4% (2017-), 51.3% (last 5y), 52.4% (last 2y), 46.2% (last 1y); 2-day up-frequency is 54.0 / 53.3 / 51.1 / 50.8 / 48.6% over the same windows. A public calendar-week table reports 56% of weeks positive since 2013 (different definition: Mon-Sun weeks, non-overlapping). The prompt never says which window or definition, so the 'outside view' is whatever the model likes. The example reference classes ('day after a +5% short-squeeze into resistance', 'week containing PCE') are worse: the model cannot compute conditional frequencies from web search and will fabricate plausible numbers, which is exactly the retrieval-fidelity failure the forecasting-evaluation literature warns about.
findings.evidence: Computed from https://github.com/ff137/bitstamp-btcusd-minute-data (script analyze.py, overlapping daily windows, strictly-greater test, zero exact ties). Calendar-week figure: https://chartrow.com/bitcoin/weekly-returns (56% positive, avg +1.84%/week, through 2026-09-09). On retrieval/leakage pitfalls: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.00723 ; on retrieval-augmented forecasting being the source of gains: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18563.
findings.fix: Have the local Python script compute and inject a BASE-RATE BLOCK each run: up-frequency at 2d and 7d for the trailing 2y and 5y, 7-day log-return s.d. for 90d/1y/2y, empirical Q3 bucket masses, and any conditional reference class you actually want (e.g., 7-day outcome after a >5% 2-day move). Prompt rule: 'Use only base rates from the BASE-RATE BLOCK. If a reference class you want is not in the block, write "not computed" and do not estimate it.' Drop the '~51-53%' text from the prompt.

findings.title: The ±4% Q3 buckets are regime-dependent, and the 'within' bucket's base rate is far from one-third
findings.issue: Whether ±4% is a sensible partition depends entirely on the vol regime. Today (30-day realized 44.3% by my calculation; Glassnode 47.25% on Sept 7) the 7-day 1 s.d. is ~6.0-6.5%, so ±4% is about ±0.65 s.d. and the buckets are reasonably balanced: empirically 53% of 7-day moves were within ±4% over the last year, 57% over two years (normal approximation at 47% vol: 46% within, 27% per tail). But the same buckets give 66% 'within' at 30% annualized vol (a level DVOL touched in May 2026 at 36) and 28% 'within' at the long-run 80% vol; the full-history share is 43%. Two consequences: (a) the prompt's 'unusually strong evidence' hedging language, if read as 'stay near equal thirds', is systematically wrong for the middle bucket; (b) Q3 forecasts across different regimes are not comparable, so pooled scoring mixes regimes. Boundary inclusivity (is exactly +4.00% 'within' or '> +4%'?) is also undefined.
findings.evidence: Computed from Bitstamp data (analyze.py: sd7 by window; bucket masses; normal-approximation table). Vol regime: https://www.kucoin.com/blog/why-bitcoin-volatility-is-historically-low-in-2026 (Glassnode 1-month realized vol 47.25% on 2026-09-07); DVOL nine-month low of 36.11 in May 2026 per https://financefeeds.com/how-the-bitcoin-implied-volatility-index-helps/ .
findings.fix: Either (a) define the buckets in vol units: 'bucket edges = anchor × exp(±1.0 × σ_7d) where σ_7d = DVOL × sqrt(7/365), stated in dollars in the output', or (b) keep ±4% but inject the current-regime empirical bucket masses from the BASE-RATE BLOCK and require the forecast to be stated as those masses plus explicit, itemized shifts. In both cases specify 'within' as closed interval [-4%, +4%], score Q3 with the Ranked Probability Score, and store σ_7d alongside each forecast so regimes can be separated at scoring time.

findings.title: The 35-65% clamp is justified only as an empirical prior, yet it is imposed by fiat, compounds documented LLM attenuation, and makes the instrument unfalsifiable
findings.issue: For Q1/Q2 a near-50% prior is defensible: every lookback window puts the up-frequency between 46% and 54%, and the risk-neutral P(up) from ATM options is ~48.7% at 47% vol over 7 days. So the clamp is unlikely to hurt Brier. But three problems remain. (1) The AIA Forecaster report found LLMs systematically attenuate probabilities and needed Platt scaling with coefficient ~1.73 to match superforecasters; a hard clamp is the opposite intervention, applied blind. (2) Combined with 'move in small steps' and 'only un-priced information may move you', the clamp creates a 50% attractor: the model can always produce 48-52% and never be wrong, which means it can never be shown to be right either (see the power finding). (3) The clamp is written as a universal rule but only makes sense for the binary questions; applied to Q3 it would force the 'within' bucket toward 35-65% when its regime base rate legitimately spans 28-66%.
findings.evidence: AIA Forecaster: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07678 (claims verified via WebSearch summaries; arxiv fetch is blocked in this container): 'LLMs systematically attenuate probabilities... Platt scaling, mathematically equivalent to log-odds extremization, effectively corrects this'; coefficient sqrt(3) from Neyman & Roughgarden 2022, summarized at https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/biL94PKfeHmgHY6qe/principled-extremizing-of-aggregated-forecasts . Base-rate range: computed from Bitstamp data. N(d2) = N(-0.5·σ√T) = N(-0.0325) ≈ 0.487: reasoning only.
findings.fix: Replace the clamp with a soft, auditable rule: 'Start from the injected base rate. Each adjustment must name one un-priced item and its log-odds shift (e.g., +0.10). Sum the shifts; report both the raw sum and the final probability. Sanity bound 20-80%; anything outside requires a named catalyst with a date.' Restrict the bound to Q1/Q2 explicitly. Pre-register that after 100 scored forecasts a Platt coefficient will be fit on the log; if it is >1 the model is under-extremizing and the rule is loosened, if <1 it is tightened. Let the data, not the prompt author, decide the shrinkage.

findings.title: Step 1 demands data the model usually cannot retrieve fresh, with no freshness gate, which invites confident stale or fabricated inputs
findings.issue: Step 1 asks for ETF daily flows, liquidations, funding, open interest, options max pain and skew, Fear & Greed, and prediction-market odds. Via web search these are typically 1-7 days stale, from secondary write-ups, and frequently unavailable; the model is told to 'cite sources, note dates' but nothing prevents a 5-day-old funding print or last week's ETF flow from being treated as current. In the forecasting literature the gain from retrieval comes from timely, relevant articles, and evaluations that ignore retrieval timing are the main source of illusory skill. Because the 48h question is dominated by information from the last few hours, stale flow data is not merely useless but actively misleading, and 'say I don't know' is not a strong enough guard against a model that found a number, just an old one.
findings.evidence: Retrieval-driven gains: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18563 (Brier 0.179 vs baseline 0.208, crowd 0.149; verified via search summary). Timing/leakage pitfalls: https://spylab.ai/blog/forecasting-pitfalls/ and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.00723 . Container tests in the harness context confirm Farside, alternative.me, Polymarket, Kalshi and CoinGecko are unreachable, so the same failure will occur in any hosted run.
findings.fix: Add a freshness gate: 'Every number must carry a source timestamp. For Q1, any input older than 24h is labelled STALE and may not move the forecast; for Q2, older than 72h. If the only value found is STALE, treat the item as missing.' Move the mechanical inputs (price, realized vol, 7d/24h change, funding if available from a no-auth endpoint) into the injected DATA BLOCK produced by the local script, and reserve web search for dated events, scheduled catalysts and central-bank calendars, which search handles well.

findings.title: Market cross-check names no instrument or conversion, so 'compare with options-implied and prediction-market odds' is not executable
findings.issue: Step 4 is the prompt's only external anchor, and the literature says it is the strongest one (AIA underperformed liquid-market consensus on its own but added information when ensembled with it). Yet the prompt does not say which market or how to turn it into P(up over 7 days). Polymarket weekly BTC markets are 'above $X' ladders, not 'up vs now'; its daily Up/Down markets resolve at 12:00 PM ET on Binance, a different instant and venue from the prompt's Coinbase resolution; Kalshi settles on a 60-second BRTI average. Options give a risk-neutral P(S_T > S_0) ≈ N(-σ√T/2), about 48.7% at 47% vol for 7 days, and a skew-adjusted number requires reading the ATM-delta and 25-delta skew from Deribit, which the model may not reach. Without this spelled out, the '>10 points' rule fires against whatever number the model happens to find.
findings.evidence: AIA vs market consensus: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07678 (verified via https://www.alphaxiv.org/overview/2511.07678v1 summary). Polymarket daily rules: https://polymarket.com/event/bitcoin-up-or-down-on-september-16-2026 ; weekly ladders: https://polymarket.com/crypto/weekly ; Kalshi settlement: https://help.kalshi.com/en/articles/13823838-crypto-markets . N(d2) figure: reasoning only.
findings.fix: Specify: 'Market-implied P(up, 7d) = delta of the Deribit BTC call at the strike nearest the anchor price for the expiry nearest anchor+7d, minus a skew note; if unavailable, use 0.49. For Q3, read the Polymarket weekly ladder for the two strikes nearest anchor×0.96 and anchor×1.04 and convert to bucket masses; if unavailable, use the injected empirical masses.' Log the market-implied value with every forecast so it can serve as the skill-score baseline.

findings.title: The questions are not decision-linked: 48h and 7-day direction has near-zero decision value for a $70k long-term holder making staged adds
findings.issue: Tetlock-style question design starts from the decision. The user's decision is whether and when to add to (or trim) a long-term position. A P(up in 7 days) that the prompt itself says must live in 35-65% cannot change that decision; a holder acting on 55% vs 45% would be trading noise at Coinbase's fee level. The decision-relevant quantities are drawdown and level probabilities: P(BTC trades ≥10% below the anchor at any point in the next 30 days), P(close below the user's next add-level within 30 days), and the 30-day 80% range. Those are also scorable with far fewer observations because the events are less balanced than 50/50. The output section's 'what this means for a long-term holder' therefore asks the model to invent a bridge from a coin-flip forecast to a decision, which is where advice-style overconfidence enters.
findings.evidence: reasoning only (base-rate computations above show every 7-day directional window between 46% and 54%; long-run 7-day s.d. 6-11% vs the user's 2-3% flip target). Superforecaster methodology reference: Schoenegger et al. 2024, https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adp1528 , which tests LLM crowds on resolvable, decision-relevant binary questions rather than asset direction.
findings.fix: Keep Q1/Q2 only as a calibration exercise and add two holder questions: 'Q4: P(Coinbase BTC-USD 1-min close ≤ anchor × 0.90 at any minute in the next 30 days)' and 'Q5: P(close ≤ user_add_level at anchor+30d)'. Replace the free-text holder advice with a fixed rule the forecast plugs into, e.g., 'add tranche k if Q4 ≥ 0.4 and current price ≤ 200-day MA', and log the rule's trigger state each week so the rule, not the prose, gets scored.

critic:forecasting-science.overall: The prompt's literature basis is real and fairly characterised (Schoenegger et al. 2024 in Science Advances, Halawi et al. 2024, and the Bridgewater AIA Forecaster report all support search-first, base-rate-first, market-anchored, logged forecasting), and its humility about short-horizon BTC direction is empirically right: every lookback window I computed puts the 2-day and 7-day up-frequency between 46% and 54%. As a forecasting instrument, however, it fails on the two things that matter most: the questions are not resolvable as written (no anchor timestamp, resolution instant, candle or tie rule, and a search-derived 'current price' can be 4-5% off the live print, which is the whole Q3 bucket width), and the weekly log has no statistical power to ever tell the user whether the model has skill (roughly 585 forecasts at 58% true skill, i.e., 11 years weekly). The fixes are mechanical and worth doing before any forecast is issued: inject a script-computed anchor, base-rate and vol block; define resolution the way Polymarket and Kalshi do; log the 80% interval and market-implied baseline; run Q1 daily; score with Brier/RPS/coverage against pre-registered baselines; and add decision-linked drawdown questions, because a 7-day direction probability confined to 35-65% cannot rationally change a long-term holder's staged-add decision.

findings.title: Probabilities never connect to an action rule; no do-nothing default
findings.issue: The prompt produces P(up) numbers, a range, and a vague line 'what this means for a long-term holder deciding on staged adds', but nowhere defines what number triggers what action. Worse, its own calibration rule (stay inside 35-65% absent unusual evidence) guarantees that nearly every week the output is ~45-55%, i.e. informationally empty for a decision, yet the reader still gets a fresh directional number to anchor on every Monday. A weekly holder prompt should be governed by an allocation/drift rule where 'do nothing' is the explicit, pre-stated default and the forecast at most nudges execution timing.
findings.evidence: Vanguard rebalancing research finds no material difference in risk-adjusted outcomes across monthly/quarterly/annual/threshold rebalancing, recommends 5-percentage-point absolute bands, and wider (5% not 2%) bands in taxable accounts; a 5% band historically produced only 3-4 rebalances per decade: https://www.bogleheads.org/wiki/Rebalancing and https://www.kitces.com/blog/best-opportunistic-rebalancing-frequency-time-horizons-vs-tolerance-band-thresholds/ (Vanguard primary PDF at corporate.vanguard.com is egress-blocked here; figures taken from search summaries).
findings.fix: Rewrite Step 5 so the FIRST line is a verdict from a fixed rule, and the forecast is subordinate. Proposed rule block for the weekly prompt: (1) INPUTS the user supplies once and updates quarterly: liquid net worth, BTC units, target BTC allocation T% and hard ceiling C%, cash needed for the next 12-24 months. (2) Each week compute current BTC % of liquid net worth. (3) DO NOTHING if within T +/- max(5 percentage points, 25% relative). Print 'DO NOTHING this week: BTC is X% of liquid net worth, inside band [lo, hi]. Next scheduled review: <date>.' (4) TRIM to T (not below) only if above the upper band; ADD to T only if below the lower band AND cash beyond the 12-24 month reserve exists. (5) The 7-day forecast may only move execution inside a 14-day window (e.g., 'band breached; forecast 58% up, execute trim in two tranches this week and next'), never create or cancel an action. (6) State explicitly: 'A forecast between 35% and 65% is not a reason to act.'

findings.title: Horizon mismatch: 48h and 7-day questions are noise for a multi-year holder and invite churn
findings.issue: Q1 (48h direction) has no bearing on a position the user intends to hold for years, and Q2/Q3 barely more. Serving a long-term holder a fresh 48-hour call every week is the behavioral-finance failure mode the prompt should be preventing: it converts a buy-and-hold investor into an attention-driven trader. The literature on retail short-horizon trading is uniformly negative, and daily BTC returns are statistically consistent with a random walk, so the 48h number cannot carry decision value even if perfectly calibrated (it will sit at ~50%).
findings.evidence: Barber & Odean (2000): the 20% of households that traded most earned 11.4%/yr vs 17.9% for the market, with overconfidence driving turnover: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=219228. BIS (2022) app-download study: ~75-81% of retail bitcoin buyers lost money, larger investors sold before declines while small investors kept buying: https://www.theblock.co/post/213372/majority-of-bitcoin-retail-investors-lost-money-in-the-last-seven-years-bis. Chague, De-Losso & Giovannetti: 97% of Brazilian day traders who persisted >300 days lost money, no evidence of learning: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3423101. Variance-ratio tests on daily BTC log returns 2013-Feb 2026 cannot reject a random walk (arXiv 2606.00071, via search; arxiv.org egress-blocked here).
findings.fix: Split the prompt in two and never mix them. HOLDER prompt (weekly): delete Q1 entirely; keep at most one price question, the 7-day three-bucket Q3, used solely for execution timing when the band rule already says act. Replace the freed slots with holder-relevant questions: (a) P(BTC drawdown > 30% and > 50% from today's price within 12 months), (b) 'Has any thesis-breaking event occurred since last quarter? (regulatory prohibition, protocol/security failure, custodian failure, personal liquidity need)' answered yes/no with citation, (c) implied 30-day vol from Deribit DVOL as the volatility budget input (DVOL/20 is a rough expected daily move; https://insights.deribit.com/exchange-updates/dvol-deribit-implied-volatility-index/). TRADER prompt (the flip pool): keep Q1/Q2 there and score them; explicitly forbid the trader prompt from referencing the $70k stack.

findings.title: No position sizing relative to net worth, cash needs, or a ceiling allocation
findings.issue: The prompt knows the user holds '$70,000 of BTC' but has no idea whether that is 3% or 60% of their liquid net worth, whether they have 12-24 months of expenses in cash, or whether the $5-10k flip pool comes out of emergency reserves. Every buy/sell suggestion is therefore unsized and unsafe: 'staged adds' for someone already at 40% of net worth in BTC is the wrong advice regardless of the forecast. The single biggest lever on this person's outcome is allocation, not weekly direction, and the prompt is silent on it.
findings.evidence: BlackRock Investment Institute, 'Sizing Bitcoin in Portfolios' (Dec 2024, reiterated June 2026): a 1-2% allocation contributes 2-5% of portfolio risk, comparable to a Magnificent Seven stock; a 4% allocation pushes BTC's risk contribution to ~14%, dominating the portfolio: https://www.ai-cio.com/news/blackrock-identifies-1-to-2-as-optimal-bitcoin-allocation/ and https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/08/30/according-to-blackrock-bitcoin-is-still-a-great-po/. Risk-contribution math is convex in allocation, so 'how much' dominates 'when'.
findings.fix: Add a mandatory INPUTS section the model must refuse to run without: liquid net worth; BTC % of liquid net worth today; target T% and ceiling C% (the user chooses; the prompt should print a reference point such as BlackRock's 1-2% and note that 10%+ makes BTC the dominant risk); months of expenses held in cash; whether the flip pool is carved from the $70k (it should not be) or from surplus cash; whether BTC is held as spot or as an ETF (tax treatment differs). Add a hard rule: 'Never recommend an ADD that pushes BTC above C% or draws cash below the 12-24 month reserve; never recommend a TRIM below T%.' Add a pre-mortem line every week: 'If BTC fell 50% from here your position would be $X, or Y% of net worth. Is that inside your written plan?' Re-confirm T and C quarterly, not weekly, to avoid target-drift by mood.

findings.title: Tax lots are ignored; any trim suggestion can silently convert long-term gains to short-term
findings.issue: The prompt's output can recommend selling but has no lot ledger, so it cannot tell whether a trim realizes long-term (0/15/20%) or short-term (10-37%) gains, cannot choose high-basis lots, and does not know that since 1 Jan 2025 lot selection must be done account-by-account and specific identification must be designated at the time of sale, not at filing. With 1099-DA cost-basis reporting mandatory from tax year 2026, mismatches between the model's suggestion and the broker's default (FIFO) will show up on a form. It also misses the one genuinely free lunch available to a spot-BTC holder: the wash-sale rule does not currently apply to directly held crypto (though it is applied by brokers to ETF shares like IBIT).
findings.evidence: Holding period and rates: https://www.vaneck.com/us/en/blogs/digital-assets/bitcoin-taxes-explained-what-investors-need-to-know-in-2026/. Per-wallet/account lot rule from 1 Jan 2025 and Rev. Proc. 2024-28 safe harbor; 1099-DA basis reporting mandatory TY2026: https://www.thetaxadviser.com/issues/2026/mar/navigating-the-form-1099-da-reporting-maze/ and https://camusocpa.com/irs-form-1099-da-the-definitive-2025-2026-guide-to-crypto-tax-reporting-compliance-cost-basis-rules-for-taxpayers/. Specific ID must be identified at time of sale; Coinbase Tax Center offers FIFO/LIFO/HIFO settings: https://chainwisecpa.com/crypto-cost-basis-methods/. Wash sale does not apply to spot crypto as of Sept 2026 (H.R. 9172 pending, not law) but brokers apply it to spot-BTC ETF shares: https://gordonlaw.com/learn/crypto-wash-sale-rule-in-2026-is-the-loophole-finally-closed/ and https://countonsheep.com/blog/bitcoin-etf-taxes-2026.
findings.fix: Add a LOT LEDGER input (per account: acquisition date, quantity, cost basis) that the user keeps in a CSV and pastes or links each week. Decision rules: (1) TRIM selects lots held >1 year with the highest basis within the same account (HIFO among long-term lots); print the estimated realized gain and its character. (2) Never sell a lot <1 year old for a rebalancing trim unless BTC exceeds 1.5x the ceiling; if a short-term lot is the only option, print the date it turns long-term and ask whether waiting is acceptable. (3) ADDs are logged as new lots with dates. (4) If any lot is underwater by >15%, print a loss-harvest option (sell and immediately rebuy, allowed for spot BTC under current law; NOT for ETF shares) with the dollar tax value, flagged 'verify with CPA; legislation pending'. (5) Set the exchange's default cost-basis method to match the ledger before the first trim, and confirm the account-by-account rule is respected.

findings.title: 'Staged adds' is baked in as the only action path, with no symmetric trim and no evidence basis
findings.issue: Step 5 asks what the forecast means 'for a long-term holder deciding on staged adds'. That framing (a) assumes the user should be accumulating, which is an allocation question the prompt has not asked, (b) offers no symmetric 'staged trim' path, so the prompt is structurally pro-buy for someone who may already be over-allocated, and (c) implies that adds should be gated by weekly forecasts, which turns dollar-cost averaging into market timing. The research on staging cash in is that it is a behavioral comfort with a cost, not an edge.
findings.evidence: Vanguard (Feb 2023), 'Cost averaging: Invest now or temporarily hold your cash?': lump sum beat cost averaging ~68% of the time over one year (MSCI World 1976-2022); cost averaging is justified mainly for investors so loss-averse they would otherwise stay in cash: https://corporate.vanguard.com/content/dam/corp/research/pdf/cost_averaging_invest_now_or_temporarily_hold_your_cash.pdf (egress-blocked here; figure via https://www.nl.vanguard/professional/vanguard-365/cost-averaging). Asymmetry point: reasoning only.
findings.fix: Replace the 'staged adds' line with a symmetric, forecast-independent execution rule: once the band rule says ADD or TRIM, execute the full amount back to target either at once or in a fixed calendar schedule the user chooses in advance (e.g., 4 equal weekly tranches), and state that the schedule is for regret-minimization, not return. Forbid the model from delaying or accelerating a scheduled tranche based on that week's P(up). If the user wants to accumulate over time as a matter of plan (not forecast), that is a monthly fixed-dollar buy that lives in the INPUTS ('planned monthly add: $N') and is executed regardless of the forecast; the weekly check only confirms it does not breach C%.

findings.title: The 'superforecaster with a strong track record' role is unearned and the scoring loop has no consequence
findings.issue: The role line asserts a track record the model does not have, and the log line collects Brier data with no rule for what happens to it. For a non-professional reader this is the most dangerous part: a confident, well-structured, cited weekly analysis reads like expertise and will be acted on, but the research on LLM forecasters shows they land roughly at the level of an unskilled crowd median and below superforecasters. Weekly forecasts constrained to 35-65% also cannot demonstrate skill for years: 52 observations a year at ~50% cannot separate skill from chance with useful confidence.
findings.evidence: Critique of Halawi 2024 / Schoenegger 2024 claims: 'state-of-the-art models perform only roughly as well as a simple median of forecasts from humans with no forecasting experience... and perform significantly worse than the median forecast of superforecasters': https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uGkRcHqatmPkvpGLq/contra-papers-claiming-superhuman-ai-forecasting (egress-blocked for fetch; quote via search summary). Halawi et al. 2024, NeurIPS: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/5a5acfd0876c940d81619c1dc60e7748-Paper-Conference.pdf. Sample-size point: reasoning only.
findings.fix: (1) Change ROLE to 'You are a forecasting assistant with NO demonstrated track record on BTC; your forecasts are provisional until scored.' (2) Add a SKILL GATE: forecasts are informational only until at least 100 resolved forecasts exist AND the rolling Brier score beats the always-50% baseline (0.25) and the 'historical base rate' baseline by a stated margin; print the current N and Brier every week. (3) Require the log to carry a resolution field and have the prompt begin each week by resolving last week's Q2/Q3 against Coinbase spot, so the score is actually maintained. (4) Add a line 'Expected value of acting on this forecast after fees and taxes' that is by construction near zero inside 35-65%, so the reader sees why the answer is do-nothing.

findings.title: Output ordering and length maximize anchoring on the P(up) number
findings.issue: The reader encounters price, catalysts, both-sides arguments and P(up) before any statement about their own position. Behaviorally, whatever number appears first becomes the anchor; a weekly reader will remember '58% up' and forget the band rule. The prompt also has no explicit separation between the $70k stack and the $5-10k flip pool, inviting mental-accounting leakage (e.g., 'topping up' the flip pool from the stack after losses, or 'adding' to the stack because the trader prompt was bullish).
findings.evidence: Reasoning only (anchoring and mental accounting are standard behavioral-finance results; no specific source fetched).
findings.fix: Reorder Step 5 to: (1) VERDICT and drift status first, in one line; (2) lots touched and tax character if any action; (3) 'What would change this verdict' (the single band breach or thesis event); (4) forecast numbers and the log line last, in small print. Cap the holder output at ~200 words. Add RULES lines: 'The long-term stack and the flip pool are separate accounts with separate rules; never transfer between them; a losing flip pool is closed, not refilled from the stack.' Add 'Quarterly review of T, C and thesis only; do not re-litigate allocation weekly.'

critic:decision-usefulness.overall: As a forecasting exercise the prompt is well-built, but as a weekly decision aid for a non-professional with $70k of BTC it is decision-useless and mildly harmful: it delivers a fresh 48-hour directional number every week with no allocation target, no drift band, no tax-lot awareness and no explicit do-nothing default, which is precisely the setup that turns holders into noise traders. The fix is to invert the hierarchy: a fixed rebalancing rule (target and ceiling as a percent of liquid net worth, act only outside a wide band, trims from long-term high-basis lots, adds only from surplus cash on a pre-set schedule) governs every week, and the forecast is demoted to an execution-timing input that is gated behind a demonstrated Brier track record. Keep the superforecaster machinery for the separate paper-traded flip pool, where short-horizon questions are actually the object of study, and wall it off from the long-term stack.

findings.title: Options 'cross-check' of P(up) is a tautology; it can only validate the distribution width (Q3), and even then risk-neutral overstates tails
findings.issue: Step 4 tells the model to compare its P(up) with 'options-implied odds' and move if they differ by >10 points. Options do not give a P(up). Under the risk-neutral measure with ~0 carry, P(S_T > S_0) = Phi(-sigma*sqrt(T)/2), which for any plausible BTC vol (35-70%) is 48.5-49.5% at 7 days and ~49.5% at 48h. So the divergence rule can never trigger for Q1/Q2 and gives the model false comfort. What implied vol actually provides is the width of the distribution, i.e. the prior for Q3 and the 80% range. And that width is biased: BTC implied vol systematically exceeds subsequently realized vol (a variance risk premium), so risk-neutral bucket masses overstate both tails. Skew (25-delta risk reversal) is the only directional information in the surface, and evidence that option order flow carries direction is modest.
findings.evidence: Risk-neutral P(up) formula: reasoning only (lognormal with zero drift). Variance risk premium in BTC: Alexander & Imeraj, 'The Bitcoin VIX and Its Variance Risk Premium', J. Alternative Investments (https://www.pm-research.com/content/iijaltinv/23/4/84) and Deribit Insights reporting 30d ATM IV over-pricing realized by ~15 vol points when the term structure is in contango (https://insights.deribit.com/industry/bitcoin-options-finding-edge-in-four-years-of-volatility-regimes/) — both via search snippets, full text not fetched. Option order-flow information: arXiv 2109.02776 'Net Buying Pressure and the Information in Bitcoin Option Trades' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.02776), snippet only. DVOL levels: 36.11 nine-month low in May 2026, 37->44 spike Jan 2026 per CME article (https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/2026/bitcoin-options-volatility-spikes-and-recovery-signals.html); September 2026 DVOL level: not found.
findings.fix: Rewrite Step 4 as: (1) Pull DVOL (or 7-day ATM IV). Compute sigma7 = IV * sqrt(7/365) and sigma48 = IV * sqrt(2/365). (2) Prior for Q3: P(within +/-4%) = 2*Phi(0.04/sigma7) - 1; tails split ~equally then tilted by skew. Worked values: DVOL 36 -> 58% within, 45 -> 48%, 60 -> 37%. (3) Because IV carries a premium, blend: sigma_used = 0.5*IV + 0.5*(30-day realized vol) before computing buckets. (4) Use 25-delta risk reversal only as a +/-2-3 point tilt on P(up), explicitly labelled weak. (5) Delete the '>10 points vs options' rule for Q1/Q2; keep a divergence check only against Polymarket/Kalshi strike-ladder markets for the same date (see finding on prediction markets), which are already in probability units.

findings.title: Fixed +/-4% buckets and a fixed 35-65% band ignore the volatility regime, which is the only thing that is actually forecastable
findings.issue: The prompt hardcodes bucket edges at +/-4% and a probability band of 35-65% regardless of regime. Direction has no autocorrelation to exploit, but volatility is strongly persistent, so the probability mass inside +/-4% swings enormously with regime and is predictable in advance. The prompt never asks for realized vol, implied vol level, or the IV term structure; it only asks for 'skew'. As written, the model will produce Q3 numbers by feel, in the one component where a quantitative prior is available.
findings.evidence: Computed from the CoinMetrics community daily series (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/coinmetrics/data/master/csv/btc.csv, through 2026-05-24, UTC closes): AR(1) of daily log returns = -0.03 to -0.07 (no directional memory) vs corr(trailing 30-day RV, next-7-day RV) = 0.41 (2015-26), 0.35 (2020-26), 0.25 (2024-26), 0.29 (Jun 2025-May 2026). 7-day return sd: 9.45% (2015-26), 8.38% (2020-26), 6.32% (2024-26), 5.22% (Jun 2025-May 2026). P(within +/-4% over 7d): 45.7% / 48.1% / 52.0% / 56.1% over the same windows; by trailing-RV tercile (2015-26): 54.8% in low-RV vs 36.7% in high-RV. 80% central 7-day range: -9.0..+12.6% (2015-26) vs -6.8..+5.7% (last 12 months). HAR persistence literature: https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7072/14/4/81 and https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/for.2989 (snippets only).
findings.fix: Add Step 1i 'Volatility regime': 7-day and 30-day realized vol (annualized, from Coinbase daily closes), DVOL, and the 7-day-vs-30-day IV term structure (contango/backwardation). Require the model to state sigma7 and sigma48 in the output BEFORE any bucket probabilities, and derive the +/-4% bucket prior and the 80% range from sigma (80% range = ref_px * exp(+/-1.28*sigma7), then adjust for skew). Better: define the buckets in sigma units (> +1 sigma7, within +/-1 sigma7, < -1 sigma7) so the question is comparable across regimes. Replace the fixed 35-65% band with a band defined in sigma terms for Q3 and keep 40-60% for Q1/Q2 unless a named un-priced catalyst exists.

findings.title: 'Max pain' and Fear & Greed have no documented value at 48h/7d horizons; one is a Friday-morning micro-effect, the other is lagged price
findings.issue: Step 1d/1e ask the model to search for options max pain and the Fear & Greed index as if they were forecasting inputs. Max pain: the only academic evidence for strike pinning is in US equities on expiration day itself, and the magnitude is tens of basis points; no academic study of BTC pinning was found, and practitioner reviews of 2026 Deribit expiries note the pin did not occur. Any effect is confined to the hours before 08:00 UTC Friday settlement and is irrelevant to a 7-day P(up). Fear & Greed: the index is constructed from price momentum, volatility and volume, so it re-counts Step 1a; the most recent study (2018-2025 data) finds returns Granger-cause the index, not the reverse, with no out-of-sample forecasting gain. Both inputs invite the model to move off the base rate on noise.
findings.evidence: Equity pinning: Ni, Pearson & Poteshman (2005), JFE 78(1), 'Stock price clustering on option expiration dates' (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304405X05000577), ~16.5 bp average expiration-day effect. BTC max pain: no academic study found; 2026 practitioner notes reporting absence of pinning: https://www.tradenzify.com/2026/06/bitcoin-options-expiry-max-pain-theory-debunked.html and https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319043/20260625/bitcoin-options-expiry-debunks-max-pain-theory-etf-outflows-rewrite-playbook.htm (non-academic, snippets only). Deribit settlement at 08:00 UTC: https://www.backquant.com/learn/max-pain (practitioner). Fear & Greed: 'Do bitcoin returns move sentiment? Evidence from the crypto fear & greed index' (2026), https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S305070062600006X — returns lead sentiment, no Granger causality from index to returns, no OOS gain (snippet only).
findings.fix: Delete 'max pain' and 'Fear & Greed' from Step 1. Replace max pain with a calendar item: 'Does the 48h or 7d window contain a monthly/quarterly Deribit expiry (last Friday, 08:00 UTC) or a CME futures expiry? If yes, note notional and the strikes with the largest OI, and widen sigma for the final 12 hours before settlement; do not shift P(up).' If Fear & Greed is retained for the human reader, force the tag 'already priced in: yes' and forbid it from moving any probability.

findings.title: Funding, open interest, liquidations and ETF flows are positioning/flow descriptors, mostly contemporaneous with price; the prompt lets them move direction
findings.issue: Step 1d bundles ETF flows, liquidations, funding and OI as 'flows & positioning' with no instruction on how they map to a probability. Evidence: spot-ETF flows explain a large share of SAME-DAY return variance and there is a feedback loop where lagged returns drive flows (return-chasing), so a big inflow print after a big up day is not new information. Farside publishes after the US close, and creations/redemptions are hedged intraday, so by the time the model searches, the impact is in the price. Funding: the only predictability evidence found is that funding predicts future FUNDING; no verified study shows funding predicts 48h/7d returns, and crypto carry returns collapsed in 2024-25. OI/liquidations: no directional predictability found; they amplify the size of moves and tell you which side is crowded. Used as written, these inputs will push P(up) around on the basis of narrative.
findings.evidence: ETF flows: Lim, 'The Price Impact of Spot Bitcoin ETF Flows' (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6592830) — flows explain ~21% of daily return variation, some next-day predictability claimed; Mazur & Polyzos (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5452994) — lagged returns drive flows; 'One year of bitcoin spot ETPs' (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165176525001417). All SSRN pages blocked by egress; snippets only. Funding predicts funding, not returns: Inan, 'Predictability of Funding Rates' (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5576424); carry Sharpe falling to negative in 2025: arXiv 2510.14435 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.14435), snippet. OI/liquidation magnitude only: arXiv 2102.04591 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.04591). Funding -> subsequent-return predictability at 48h/7d: not found.
findings.fix: Collapse 1d into one 'Leverage & crowding' block with four numbers: perp funding percentile vs trailing 90 days; OI in BTC terms and vs 30-day average; CME 3-month annualized basis (contango/backwardation); 24h long vs short liquidation ratio. Its permitted outputs are (a) a variance multiplier (crowded + high OI -> widen sigma), and (b) tail asymmetry ('crowded longs -> fatter left tail'). Cap its effect on P(up) at +/-3 points. Tag ETF flow as 'already priced in: yes' unless the flow print postdates the reference price timestamp. Remove 'liquidations' as a stand-alone item (it is the same information as OI change).

findings.title: No reference-price or timestamp discipline: 'higher than current price' is undefined when the price came from a stale search snippet
findings.issue: Q1/Q2 resolve 'against Coinbase BTC-USD spot' relative to 'the current price', but Step 1a gets that price from web search, which is minutes to hours stale. Post-ETF daily close-to-close sd is ~2.2-2.5% and 48h sd ~3.0-3.4%, so a one-hour-old reference can already be off by 0.5-1%, a material fraction of the 48h distribution; P(up vs a stale reference) is then not ~50% and the Brier log becomes unscorable. The log line lacks issue timestamp, reference source and resolution timestamps. Also, the prompt compares against Polymarket/Kalshi, which settle on Chainlink and CF Benchmarks respectively, not Coinbase; usually a few bp, but it matters at the +/-4% boundary.

findings.title: Calendar and session effects (weekend, US hours, CPI/FOMC days, expiries) are missing, and they are where the 48h variance actually lives

findings.title: The scoring plan cannot detect directional skill at weekly cadence; score the distribution (Q3, 80% interval) instead, and compute the base rate rather than hardcode it
findings.issue: The prompt promises Brier-scored accountability but at one forecast per week the log will not distinguish a skilled forecaster from a coin flip for years: detecting 55% vs 50% directional accuracy at 80% power needs ~780 resolved forecasts (15 years weekly); 60% vs 50% needs ~200 (about 4 years). Meanwhile the hardcoded '~51-53%' base rate is roughly right for the current regime but wrong for other windows and the prompt gives no window. The user's actual decision (staged adds to a $70k long-term position, reviewed weekly) does not need a 48h direction call at all.

Replace '~51-53%' with 'compute P(up 2d), P(up 7d), sigma7 and P(within +/-4%) from the last 2 years of Coinbase daily closes and state the window used'. critic:quant-microstructure.overall: The prompt's process scaffolding is sound, but its input list is mostly inherited from crypto-Twitter dashboards rather than from evidence: max pain, Fear & Greed, liquidations and funding have no documented directional value at 48h/7d, ETF flows are largely contemporaneous and return-chasing, and the "options-implied odds" cross-check is a tautology for P(up) because implied vol prices width, not direction. The one thing that is genuinely forecastable — the volatility regime, which moves P(within ±4%) from roughly 37% to 58% and is strongly persistent — is not asked for at all, and the fixed ±4% buckets, fixed 35–65% band, stale reference price and calendar-blind 48h window all follow from that omission. Rebuilding the prompt around "compute sigma from realized and implied vol, scale it by the window calendar (weekend/CPI/FOMC/expiry), report P(up) as the base rate ±3 points unless a named un-priced catalyst exists, and score the distribution rather than the coin flip" would make it both more honest and, for the weekly $70k position review, more useful.

findings.title: Weekly cadence plus 35-65% clamp means Q1/Q2 Brier scores cannot separate skill from a coin flip for years
findings.issue: A weekly run with a 48h question is internally coherent (Q1 resolves five days before the next run) but statistically wasteful: it yields 52 Q1 and 52 Q2 samples per year. With forecasts confined to 35-65%, the maximum expected Brier gain over the constant-0.5 baseline is (p-0.5)^2 per question: 0.0025 at 55/45, 0.01 at 60/40, 0.0225 at the 65/35 limit. Monte Carlo of a perfectly calibrated forecaster vs the 0.5 baseline (paired one-sided t-test, alpha 0.05): at weekly cadence a 60/40-skill forecaster is detected with 18% power after 1 year and 27% after 2 years; a 55/45 forecaster reaches only 24% power after 7 years. At daily cadence (365/yr) 60/40 skill reaches 59% power after 1 year and 87% after 2. The 48h horizon also does not serve the stated user of the weekly run (a long-term holder doing staged adds); it is the flip-pool's horizon.

Daily 'forecast' run (13:00 UTC, same schema, prompt_version tag 'daily'): Q1 and Q2, which gives 365 overlapping samples per year for calibration work; because 7d windows overlap, compute confidence intervals with a block bootstrap (block = 7 daily runs) rather than i.i.d. standard errors. State in the prompt header that the scoring program's purpose for the first 26 weeks is calibration diagnostics (reliability table over bins 35-45/45-55/55-65), not edge detection, and that no 'we beat the baseline' claim is made until the block-bootstrap 90% CI of the Brier difference excludes 0. Run order each cycle must be: resolve -> score -> forecast, and inject the rolling scorecard (n, mean Brier vs each baseline, reliability table) into the next prompt so the model can self-correct.

findings.title: No scoring procedure or baselines are defined; 'Brier' is undefined for the ordered 3-bucket Q3 and a uniform-1/3 baseline is a strawman
findings.issue: The prompt says the forecaster is 'scored by Brier score' but never says how Q3 (three ordered buckets), the 80% range, or the key levels are scored, and names no reference forecast. Binary Brier only covers Q1/Q2. For Q3, the multi-category Brier ranges 0-2 and ignores ordering; the ranked probability score respects it. The obvious naive baseline for Q3 (1/3 each) is easy to beat and hides real skill differences: on the last 52 non-overlapping weeks of the repo's hourly data, uniform-1/3 scores multi-category Brier 0.667 while a climatology of 2023-now bucket frequencies (below -4%: 19.0%, within: 55.5%, above +4%: 25.6%) scores 0.597. Persistence (sign of last window) hit-rate on the same data is 0.48-0.61, i.e. roughly a coin flip, so it should be included as a soft probabilistic baseline rather than a hard 0/1 forecast.
findings.evidence: https://www.metaculus.com/help/scores-faq/ (baseline score vs 50% / 1-N); https://metricgate.com/docs/ranked-probability-score-categorical/ (RPS for ordered categories); https://otexts.com/fpp3/distaccuracy.html and https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf (interval/Winkler score is proper); local computation on /home/user/crushpaper/btc-lab/data/btcusd_1h_bitstamp.csv.gz
findings.fix: Add a SCORING section to the prompt (informational for the model) and implement it in a scoring script. Per question: Q1/Q2 binary Brier (p-y)^2. Q3: report both multi-category Brier sum_k (p_k - y_k)^2 and RPS = (1/(K-1)) * sum_k (F_k - Y_k)^2 over cumulative probabilities ordered down/within/up. Range: coverage indicator and Winkler interval score with alpha=0.2 in return-percent units. Baselines computed by the script from the candle cache at each T0: (a) constant 0.5 / uniform 1/3; (b) climatology = trailing-365d fraction of up windows and trailing-2y bucket frequencies; (c) persistence = 0.5 + 0.1*sign(previous same-horizon return); (d) vol-model buckets from N(0, sigma_7d) with sigma_7d = hourly realized sd * sqrt(168), and an 80% range of +/-1.28*sigma_7d. Aggregate per prompt_version: n, mean score, Brier skill score BSS = 1 - BS/BS_ref against each baseline, reliability table, block-bootstrap 90% CI. Include a fixed minimum-n rule in the scorecard output (n >= 52 before showing a reliability table, n >= 200 before any 'edge' language).

critic:operations-scoring.overall: As a forecasting prompt v1 is well-founded, but as a recurring automated scoring process it is not runnable: its log line is unparseable, its reference and resolution prices are undefined and unfetchable from the environment that runs it, and it names a Brier score without any baseline, procedure for the ordered Q3 buckets, or versioning. The weekly cadence is coherent in timing but statistically hollow, since 52 samples a year of forecasts clamped to 35-65% cannot distinguish skill from a coin flip within any practical horizon; Q1 belongs on the daily flip-pool schedule and the weekly run should be scored for calibration, not edge. Adopting the JSON log schema, the local resolver as sole price authority, script-injected base rates, and the baseline-relative scoring procedure above would make v2 a process whose results can actually be believed.

findings.title: The scoring loop cannot validate anything for ~2 years, and the 35-65% clamp guarantees no-skill output
findings.issue: v1 admits weekly BTC direction is 'close to a coin flip' and then clamps P(up) to 35-65% unless evidence is 'unusually strong'. In practice the model will emit 50-58% every week, whose Brier score is ~0.25, the no-skill baseline. Distinguishing a 0.02 Brier improvement at 95% confidence takes on the order of 100 resolved questions; weekly, that is two years of logging. Worse, on a 30-question sample a forecaster whose true score is 0.21 can post 0.16 by luck, so after six months the user is more likely to be fooled into trusting the prompt than to learn it has no edge. Q1 (48h) is the least forecastable and least relevant question for a long-term holder and only adds noise to the log. Variance-ratio tests on daily BTC log returns from Jan 2013 to Feb 2026 cannot reject a random walk, so the base case is that there is nothing here to score.
