The 'priced in?' tag is a good idea in principle but the model has no way to verify it and will assign 'partly' to almost everything.
findings.evidence: Fear & Greed no OOS value: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S305070062600006X. Max pain weak at weekly horizon and June 2026 divergence: https://www.tradenzify.com/2026/06/bitcoin-options-expiry-max-pain-theory-debunked.html and https://www.kucoin.com/blog/en-bitcoin-options-max-pain-price-how-expiring-options-shape-btc-short-term-trends.
findings.fix: Delete (d), (e), (f) and Step 3. Replace with: 'List at most two dated, scheduled events inside the 7-day window that the market may not have fully priced. If you cannot name one with a date and a consensus number from the fact sheet, write NONE and output the base rate unchanged.'

findings.title: Q3 and the 80% range are volatility questions the prompt lets the model guess
findings.issue: The ±4% bucket probabilities and the 'central 80% range' are almost entirely determined by the current vol regime, not by any directional view. Using published realized-vol readings: at 47.25% annualized (Glassnode, 7 Sept 2026) the 1-week sigma is ~6.5%, so P(within ±4%) is ~46%; at 27.2% (11 Aug 2026) sigma is ~3.8% and P(within ±4%) is ~71% (assuming roughly normal log returns). The correct answer moved 25 points in one month on vol alone. Nothing in v1 asks for that calculation, so the model will emit something like 30/45/25 by feel and the log will be scoring arithmetic errors, not judgment.
findings.evidence: Realized vol readings: https://www.kucoin.com/blog/why-bitcoin-volatility-is-historically-low-in-2026 (47.25% on 7 Sept 2026; 27.2% on 11 Aug 2026). Bucket arithmetic: reasoning only. DVOL as the implied-vol source: https://insights.deribit.com/exchange-updates/dvol-deribit-implied-volatility-index/.
findings.fix: Have the local script compute the buckets and the 80% range mechanically from DVOL (fallback: 30-day realized vol) and put them in the fact sheet. The prompt's only job on Q3 is to say whether a scheduled event in the window justifies widening the range, and by how much, with the reason.

findings.title: The 'staged adds' bullet turns a coin-flip into weekly action on a $70k position, which is the documented harm
findings.issue: Step 5 asks what the forecast 'means for a long-term holder deciding on staged adds'. Every serious dataset says the damage to retail investors comes from decision frequency, not from bad individual calls: the most active quintile in Barber-Odean earned 11.4% vs 17.9% for the market; the BIS estimates 73-81% of retail BTC buyers lost money on their initial investments; retail crypto traders in the eToro sample chase momentum in crypto even when they are contrarian in stocks. A weekly prompt that ends with a buy/sell lean is a machine for generating exactly that behaviour. It also has tax teeth: any sale of BTC held one year or less is taxed at ordinary rates up to 37%, and selling long-term lots restarts the clock on the rebuy; a wash-sale bill (H.R. 9172, introduced June 2026) is pending. The 'not financial advice' line does nothing because the user has explicitly asked for buy/sell suggestions.
findings.evidence: Barber & Odean: https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/odean/papers%20current%20versions/individual_investor_performance_final.pdf. BIS: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-16/vast-majority-of-retail-investors-in-bitcoin-lost-money-bis-says. Momentum chasing: https://www.nber.org/papers/w31317. Tax: https://statecalc.com/blog/crypto-tax-guide-2026/ and https://tokentax.co/blog/wash-sale-trading-in-crypto.
findings.fix: Remove the bullet. Replace with a pre-committed policy the user writes once (e.g. fixed DCA amount on a fixed date; rebalance only if BTC exceeds X% of net worth; never sell lots under 12 months old). The weekly run's only permitted output on the position is 'Policy check: no action' or 'Policy trigger hit: <rule>'; the forecast may not override it.

findings.title: v1 is being pointed at two incompatible jobs; it has nothing to offer the 2-3% flip pool
findings.issue: The prompt says 'not a trader', but the surrounding request wants it to feed a $5-10k pool flipped daily for 2-3%. A weekly P(up)=55% has no bearing on a strategy whose outcome is decided by fees, stop placement and path, not direction. Two secondary sources report Coinbase Advanced entry-tier US fees of 0.50% maker / 0.90% taker after the 16 Sept 2026 restructuring (primary page blocked from here, not verified); the prior schedule was 0.40/0.60. Either way a taker round trip costs 1.2-1.8%, which consumes most of a 2% target before slippage. The base rates for this activity are the worst in finance: 97% of Brazilians who persisted 300+ sessions lost money; fewer than 1% of Taiwan day traders were reliably profitable net of fees; in a 25k-account retail sample 82% lost money despite most having >50% win rates because losers averaged -2.8% vs winners +1.2%. An LLM narrative forecast bolted onto that will make it worse, not better.
findings.evidence: Fees: https://www.securities.io/coinbase-lowers-advanced-trading-fees-with-tiers-starting-at-10-000/ (secondary; primary Coinbase page egress-blocked). Chague et al.: https://www.tradicted.com/research/chagu-day-2020/. Taiwan and win-rate data: https://medium.com/@faisal_haroon/i-reviewed-every-major-day-trading-study-from-the-last-25-years-the-data-is-devastating-4b116273b956 and https://www.investing.com/analysis/how-the-top-1-of-traders-think-databacked-lessons-from-25k-accounts-200670119.
findings.fix: Keep v1 (or its successor) strictly for the holder. The flip pool gets a separate, fully mechanical, fee-inclusive paper-trading backtest on the user's machine with no LLM in the signal path; the only LLM role there is summarizing the simulation's realized results against a buy-and-hold control. Present the 1.5% vs 2% vs 3-5% comparison as net-of-fees expectancy, not as gross targets.

findings.title: Hard-coded base rate is unverified and the design-basis citations overclaim
findings.issue: v1 bakes in 'historical up-frequency ~51-53%'. One data table reports BTC positive in 56% of weeks from 2013 to Sept 2026; the true figure depends heavily on the window chosen, and hard-coding it means the model echoes the prompt instead of computing it. The preamble cites Schoenegger/Tetlock, Halawi and AIA as if they licensed the exercise, but those results are: LLM ensemble statistically indistinguishable from a human crowd on 31 event questions; Halawi's retrieval system at 0.179 Brier vs crowd 0.149 (worse than crowd), zero-shot near chance; AIA matches superforecasters on ForecastBench but lags liquid market consensus (0.108 vs 0.098); Lu 2025 has o3 at 0.1352 vs superforecasters at 0.0225 on Metaculus. Paleka et al. and the FutureSearch critique argue even these are inflated by temporal leakage. None tested 48h or 7d asset-price direction.
findings.evidence: 56% of weeks positive: https://chartrow.com/bitcoin/weekly-returns. Schoenegger: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adp1528. Halawi: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.18563. AIA: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07678. Lu 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04562. Critiques: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.00723 and https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uGkRcHqatmPkvpGLq/contra-papers-claiming-superhuman-ai-forecasting.
findings.fix: Have the script compute the 7-day up-rate and 1-sigma move from the last 3 years of weekly closes and pass them in the fact sheet; the prompt reads them, never states them. Rewrite the preamble to the honest claim: 'Retrieval-augmented LLMs roughly match human crowds on event questions and lag liquid markets; there is no evidence of edge on short-horizon price direction, so this prompt defaults to market-implied odds.'

findings.title: Step 4 has the burden of proof backwards, and acquiescence bias will skew P(up) high
findings.issue: v1 lets the model form its own probability and only 'explain or move toward' the market if it differs by more than 10 points. Given AIA lags liquid markets and Polymarket already runs weekly BTC markets, a 10-point tolerance is enormous relative to any plausible edge. Separately, Schoenegger et al. documented acquiescence bias in LLM forecasters (a tendency to lean 'yes'); asking only 'Will BTC be higher?' invites a systematic upward drift in P(up) that the log will not detect for years.
findings.evidence: AIA vs market consensus: https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07678. Acquiescence bias: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adp1528. Weekly markets exist: https://polymarket.com/crypto/weekly.
findings.fix: Invert the rule: 'The market-implied weekly probability from the fact sheet is your forecast. You may deviate by at most 5 points, only by naming one dated, un-priced scheduled event.' Also require the model to state P(lower) independently and reconcile the two before writing the log line.

critic:red-team.overall: Scrap v1 as a forecasting engine: weekly BTC direction is the near-coin-flip the prompt itself concedes, its scoring loop cannot separate skill from luck for roughly 100 weeks, and most of Step 1 will arrive stale or confabulated through web search while its sentiment and max-pain inputs have no documented predictive value at this horizon. The minimal useful version is a weekly position-hygiene check fed by a deterministic local fact sheet: price context, a mechanically computed 1-week implied range and ±4% buckets, the dated catalyst calendar, the market-implied weekly odds, and a pre-committed rules check that outputs 'no action' by default; the 2-3% flip pool gets a separate fee-inclusive mechanical simulation with no LLM in the signal path. Keep from v1 the ROLE's humility, base-rate-first structure (computed, not hard-coded), the catalyst calendar (Step 1g), the market cross-check (inverted so the market is the default), the facts-versus-judgment rule, 'say I don't know', and the one-line log; drop Q1, Step 3, Step 1 (d)(e)(f), and the 'staged adds' bullet.

research:retail-profitability.summary: Every large-sample, account-level study of frequent retail trading finds the same shape: a large majority lose money after costs, the losses are driven mostly by fees/spreads and leverage rather than bad gross calls, persistence does not produce learning, and the small profitable minority (roughly 1-5%) is dominated by well-capitalised or systematic traders. Brazil equity-futures day traders: 97% of the 1,551 who persisted >300 days lost money; 1.1% out-earned minimum wage (Chague et al. 2020). Taiwan: fewer than 1% of day traders predictably profitable net of fees over 1992-2006; in any six-month window >8 in 10 lose (Barber/Odean team). Regulators: ESMA found 74-89% of retail CFD accounts lose; FCA 82%; ASIC still 68% (A$458m lost in 2023-24) even after leverage caps, and caps cut aggregate losses 91%, showing leverage is the main destroyer. Crypto-specific evidence is thinner but consistent: BIS finds a majority of crypto-app users in almost every country lost on bitcoin 2015-2022 (81% under a $100/month DCA assumption); on-chain Hyperliquid samples show ~74-86% of perp traders losing with median PnL -$67 and win-rate scaling with account size; surveys report 84% of first-year crypto traders losing (n=1,005, Aug 2025) and 38% of US crypto sellers realising losses (n>1,400, Jan 2023). Behavioural studies (JFE 2024 eToro; Review of Finance 2022 German bank; JPMC Institute; Cleveland Fed 2026) show retail crypto buyers chase momentum and enter after price spikes. For the user's 2-3% flip plan, fees are decisive: Kraken Pro's base tier costs 0.50-0.80% per round trip and Coinbase Advanced's entry tier reportedly 1.0-2.4% (conflicting figures after the Sept 16, 2026 change), so a 1.5% target can be half-consumed by fees before slippage and short-term-capital-gains tax. The one counterpoint (Manahov 2024) is a millisecond-data strategy backtest, not retail account outcomes. No peer-reviewed study of realised net returns for retail BTC spot day traders was found.

claims.claim: Chague, De-Losso and Giovannetti tracked all 19,646 individuals who began day trading Brazilian equity futures in 2013-2015; of the 1,551 who persisted for more than 300 trading days, 97% lost money net of fees, only 1.1% earned more than the Brazilian minimum wage, only 0.5% earned more than a bank teller's starting salary, and the single best trader averaged US$310/day with a daily standard deviation of US$2,560. The authors found no evidence of learning by day trading.

Barber, Lee, Liu and Odean ('The cross-section of speculator skill', Journal of Financial Markets 2014), using all Taiwan Stock Exchange day trading 1992-2006, find that less than 1% of the day-trader population predictably and reliably earns positive abnormal returns net of fees; the top 500 ranked day traders earned 61.3 bp/day before fees (37.9 bp after), while bottom-ranked traders earned -11.5 bp before fees (-28.9 bp after).

Barber, Lee, Liu and Odean (2004, 'Do Individual Day Traders Make Money? Evidence from Taiwan', 1995-1999 data): heavy day traders earn gross profits (NT$36.4m mean daily) but after transaction costs incur net losses (NT$68.9m per day); in a typical six-month period more than eight out of ten day traders lose money, i.e. only about 20% are profitable in any six-month window after costs.

'Learning Fast or Slow?' (Barber, Lee, Liu, Odean, Zhang; Review of Asset Pricing Studies 2020), analysing 3.7 billion TWSE transactions 1992-2006: day traders lost on average about 23.9 bp per day net of fees (about -7 bp gross, so costs more than triple the loss); aggregate day-trader performance was negative in 14 of 15 years; survival rates were 44% at one year, 24% at two, 15% at three; profitable day traders were consistently only about 5% of active traders; learning exists but is 'slow, suboptimal and costly'.

Barber and Odean ('Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth', Journal of Finance 2000): among 66,465 US discount-brokerage households 1991-1996, the average household earned 16.4%/yr with 75% annual turnover while the market returned 17.9%; the highest-turnover quintile earned only 11.4%/yr. Overconfidence-driven overtrading is the explanation.

BIS Bulletin 69 'Crypto shocks and retail losses' (Cornelli, Doerr, Frost, Gambacorta; 20 Feb 2023, first reported Nov 2022): using crypto-app download data for 95 countries over Aug 2015-Dec 2022, a majority of crypto app users in nearly all economies lost money on their bitcoin holdings; under the assumption that each new user bought $100 of bitcoin in the install month and each month thereafter, 81% would have lost money (press coverage summarises as 'about three-quarters'); during the Terra/Luna and FTX crashes large/sophisticated investors sold while smaller retail investors bought.
Bloomberg Law summary of the BIS study: about 75% of retail buyers of bitcoin lost money; most app downloads occurred when BTC was above $20,000; roughly 40% of users were men under 35.

ESMA (product-intervention decision agreed 23 March 2018): national regulators' analyses of CFD trading across EU jurisdictions show 74-89% of retail accounts typically lose money, with average losses per client ranging from EUR 1,600 to EUR 29,000; ESMA cited excessive leverage and a structural disparity between expected return and risk of loss.

FCA consultation CP16/40 (Dec 2016): in a sample of eight CFD firms, 82% of clients lost money and the average result per client account was a loss of GBP 2,200; this evidence led to the FCA's 2019 retail CFD restrictions.

ASIC media release 20-254MR (Oct 2020): reviews in 2017, 2019 and 2020 found most retail clients lose money trading CFDs; during the volatile five weeks of March-April 2020 the retail clients of a sample of 13 CFD issuers made a net loss of more than A$774 million.

ASIC 22-082MR: the March 2021 CFD product intervention order (leverage caps etc.) reduced aggregate retail CFD losses by 91%, from about A$372 million to A$33 million per quarter on average; the order was extended to 23 May 2027. This is direct evidence that leverage, not trade selection, drives the bulk of retail short-term trading losses.

ASIC Report 828 (January 2026) and coverage of it: even after leverage caps, in 2023-24 more than 133,000 people, 68% of retail CFD clients, lost more than A$458 million; ASIC also secured roughly A$36-40 million in refunds after finding conduct failures across the sector.

Current mandatory broker risk-warning disclosures (12-month rolling loss rates): Plus500 82% of retail CFD accounts lose money (March 2026), IG 69% (August 2026), eToro about 50-51% (May 2026); across brokers the disclosed range is roughly 51-89%.

On-chain analysis of 10,000 randomly sampled Hyperliquid depositor wallets over 30 days of data pulled from the public API in November 2024: 73.8% were losing, 16.5% profitable, 9.7% break-even; median PnL was -$67; 40.6% of wallets stopped trading within the 30 days and 66.4% of those quitters were unprofitable; win rate scales with account size (about 15% for accounts under $1k, near even odds only around $1M).

Hyperdash sample data reported by The Coin Republic (16 June 2025) and BeInCrypto: only about 135-166 of 1,000 sampled Hyperliquid perpetual-futures traders were profitable, i.e. roughly 84-86% losing, on a venue then doing about $188 billion in volume; other analyses put the losing share at about 75% of addresses.

NFTevening online-panel survey of 1,005 retail crypto traders (fielded 8 August 2025, respondents who traded in their first year): 84% lost money in their first year, 58% lost nearly all of their starting capital, 54% cited day trading as the main cause, 1 in 3 quit within six months, and 86% kept trading despite losses. Non-academic, self-reported.
LendingTree survey of more than 1,400 US consumers (published 30 Jan 2023): of Americans who had sold crypto, 38% sold for less than they paid, 28% for more, and 13% broke even.

Kogan, Makarov, Niessner and Schoar ('Are Cryptos Different? Evidence from Retail Trading', Journal of Financial Economics 2024), using 200,000 eToro retail traders: the same individuals who trade contrarian in stocks and gold trade momentum-like (buy after price rises) in cryptocurrencies; the difference is not explained by investor characteristics, inattention, fees or lottery preferences.

Hackethal, Hanspal, Lammer and Rink ('Characteristics and Portfolio Behavior of Bitcoin Investors', Review of Finance 2022), using German online-bank administrative data: crypto investors are active traders, prone to investment biases and hold risky portfolios, and substantially increase log-in and trading activity after their first crypto purchase.

JPMorgan Chase Institute (2025): 17% of active Chase checking-account users invested in crypto between Jan 2017 and May 2025; crypto involvement rises in waves during periods of rising prices, with recent upticks around March and November 2024 coinciding with new bitcoin all-time highs, i.e. retail entry follows price rather than leads it.

Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland working paper (14 July 2026), a randomised survey experiment: showing households bitcoin's prior 12-month return raised the probability of reporting crypto ownership by about 2.4 percentage points and raised desired crypto allocation by about 2 points (about 47% relative to the 4.3% control allocation), with actual subsequent purchases up about 2.5 points, supporting a return-chasing feedback loop.

Counterpoint: Manahov ('The rapid growth of cryptocurrencies: How profitable is trading in digital money?', International Journal of Finance & Economics 29(2), April 2024), using millisecond data for BTC, ETH, XRP, LTC, DASH and the CRIX/CCI30 indices, reports that high-frequency trading strategies generate significant profits after reasonable transaction costs. This is a strategy backtest at sub-second frequency, not evidence about retail account outcomes, and is not replicable at retail latency or retail fee tiers.

A vendor study by AI-trading lab PiP World (reported 25 Nov 2025) claiming 8 million traders and 295 million trades over 27 years: 74-89% of retail traders lost money 1998-2025 and only 11-26% avoided losses. Not peer reviewed; methodology not published in the coverage; treat as marketing-grade.

Secondary 2026 compilations (e.g. Paper Trading Journal, QuantifiedStrategies, Traders Union) repeat figures such as '10-15% of day traders profitable in a single year, 1-3% over three or more years' and '73-81% of retail crypto investors have likely incurred losses'; the crypto range appears to be lifted from the BIS bulletin and the day-trading ranges have unclear provenance.

Fee drag on the flip plan (Kraken): Kraken Pro spot fees at the base tier (under $10,000 30-day volume) are 0.25% maker / 0.40% taker in 2026, so a round trip costs 0.50% (maker both legs) to 0.80% (taker both legs) before spread and slippage; since July 2026 tiers can also be reached via assets on platform.

Fee drag on the flip plan (Coinbase): Coinbase announced a revised Advanced fee structure on 16 Sept 2026 with tiers starting at $10,000 volume (down from $25,000) and USDC balances counting toward tiers; reports of the US entry tier conflict (0.50% maker / 0.90% taker per one summary vs 0.60% maker / 1.20% taker per another, dropping to 0.25% / 0.40% at $10k-$50k). Either way the entry-tier round trip is roughly 1.0-2.4%, which consumes half to more than all of a 1.5-2% profit target.

Aggregate Hyperliquid data cited by TechFlow/HTX: roughly 75% of addresses are in loss and the average daily PnL across all traders is about -$5,600; profitable traders were characterised as running systematic high-frequency strategies, placing large high-conviction bets, or using algorithmic execution.

open_questions: No peer-reviewed study was found that measures realised net-of-fee returns of retail bitcoin SPOT day traders from exchange account data; the closest analogues are Brazil/Taiwan equity-futures day traders, CFD accounts, and on-chain perp-DEX wallets (Hyperliquid). Korean (Upbit/Bithumb), Coinbase and Robinhood account-level studies: not found.

Exact Coinbase Advanced US entry-tier maker/taker rates after the 16 Sept 2026 change are reported inconsistently (0.50/0.90% vs 0.60/1.20%); the page could not be fetched. The user should read the fee tier shown in their own account before the simulator's fee parameter is fixed.

The BIS bulletin's widely quoted '73-81% of users lost money' range could not be confirmed from result text; only 'a majority' and the 81% (under $100/month DCA) figure and 'about three-quarters' press summaries surfaced.
ASIC's 2019 REP 626 exact percentage of retail CFD clients losing money was not found (only 'most' and the 2023-24 68% figure from REP 828).

FCA Cryptoassets Consumer Research 2024 (Wave 5) and 2025 (Wave 6) proportions of holders who lost money or regret buying were not extractable; only ownership falling to 8% (Dec 2025) surfaced. Full PDFs are blocked.

Hyperliquid analyses (ENVY Protocol 10k-wallet sample; Hyperdash 1,000-trader sample) are unrefereed and the Hyperdash sampling method is unknown; results also cover leveraged perps, not spot, so they overstate losses relative to an unleveraged spot flip.
'Learning Fast or Slow?' figures (-23.9 bp/day net, ~5% profitable per year) were taken from a secondary summary; the SSRN abstract itself could not be fetched to confirm the exact numbers.
No study in this sweep tests the specific strategy class the user proposes (fixed 1.5-5% take-profit mean-reversion flips on BTC); that belongs to a separate strategy/backtest sweep.

US tax treatment of frequent crypto flips (short-term capital gains at ordinary rates; whether wash-sale rules now apply to crypto in 2026) was outside this sweep and materially lowers after-tax net of any positive result.

Whether the eToro-style behavioural findings (momentum-chasing in crypto) translate into measurably worse crypto P&L for the same traders was not reported in the result text of Kogan et al.; the paper may contain performance numbers not visible here.

research:costs-and-taxes.summary:
COSTS-AND-TAXES SWEEP (US individual, BTC spot, Sept 2026). Method: 15 distinct WebSearch queries; every WebFetch attempt (Coinbase, Kraken, Binance.US, IRS, congress.gov, govinfo, Kaiko, Tax Foundation, and ~15 secondary hosts) was blocked by the egress proxy, so all claims rest on search-result extracts, not on directly read official pages. Treat exchange fee numbers as "verify on the official page before trading".

FEES. Kraken Pro base tier (<$10K 30-day volume): 0.25% maker / 0.40% taker; since July 9, 2026 tier is set by spot volume OR assets-on-platform, whichever is better. Binance.US: 0% maker / 0.02% taker on all spot pairs for all users, no tiers (announced Apr 22, 2026); some reports say 0.01% taker on core USD pairs. Coinbase Advanced base tier is CONFLICTING across 2026 sources: "Intro 1" 0.60% maker / 1.20% taker (with Intro 2 at >=$1K 0.35/0.75 and Advanced 1 at >=$10K 0.25/0.40) vs older 0.40/0.60 vs one report of 0.50/0.90; what is consistent is that the >=$10K tier is 0.25/0.40 and the $10K threshold was lowered from $25K. Coinbase simple/retail trade carries ~0.50% spread markup on top of fees; Coinbase One waives simple-trade fees only up to $500/mo (Basic) or $10K/mo (Preferred) and spread still applies. BTC-USD top-of-book spread is negligible next to fees: Kaiko reports ~0.3 bps Coinbase, ~0.1 bps Kraken, ~1.9 bps Bitstamp (date not confirmed), and ~3 bps on Binance.US when its liquidity was poor.

ARITHMETIC (computed here from sourced fee levels, $7,500 position, 2.00% gross target). Round-trip cost = buy fee + sell fee + ~one spread. Coinbase base tier taker-both at 1.20%: 2.40% RT, which is 120% of the target (net loss on a "winning" trade). At 0.60% taker both legs (Coinbase alt base, or Coinbase >=$10K / Kraken base taker at 0.40%): 1.20% RT eats 60%, 0.80% RT eats 40%. Kraken/Coinbase-Advanced-1 maker both legs (0.25%): 0.50% RT eats 25%, net ~1.50%. Binance.US: 0.04-0.07% RT eats 2-3%, net ~1.93%. Break-even win rate with symmetric +2%/-2% target/stop: 0.80% RT needs 70%; 0.50% needs 62.5%; 0.04% needs 51%. A 1.5% target is only viable at sub-0.1% RT costs; at 0.5-0.8% RT costs fees consume 33-53% of a 1.5% target. Coinbase simple trade (spread + fee) makes a 2% flip structurally negative.

TAXES. Every flip is a short-term capital gain/loss taxed at ordinary rates (10-37%; 2026 single brackets per Rev. Proc. 2025-32: 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700, 24% to $201,775, 32% to $256,225, 35% to $640,600) plus 3.8% NIIT if MAGI > $200K single / $250K MFJ (top combined 40.8%). Wash-sale rule (IRC 1091) does NOT currently apply to crypto, so flip losses are deductible even with immediate rebuy, BUT this is actively changing: H.R. 9172 (introduced June 8, 2026; as drafted applies to dispositions after introduction) and H.R. 10357 Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, which passed House Ways and Means 38-5 on Sept 16, 2026 and extends wash-sale and constructive-sale rules to digital assets; neither is law yet and H.R. 10357's wash-sale effective date was not found. Form 1099-DA: gross proceeds reported for 2025 sales; cost basis reported for "covered" assets acquired on/after Jan 1, 2026 and held at the same broker (forms arrive early 2027); taxpayer remains responsible for basis. Since Jan 1, 2025 basis is tracked wallet-by-wallet/account-by-account (Treas. Reg. 1.1012-1(j)); FIFO is the default unless specific identification is made at/before sale; Notice 2026-20 (Mar 17, 2026) extends Notice 2025-7 relief through Dec 31, 2026 letting taxpayers make specific ID in their own books rather than through the broker, and broker-reported 2026 basis may not match, creating a reconciliation burden. Critical practical consequence: if the $5-10K flip pool sits in the same exchange account as the $70K long-term stack, FIFO will by default sell the OLDEST (likely lowest-basis, long-term) lots on every flip, converting long-term gains into realized taxable events; keep the flip pool in a separate account/sub-account or use standing specific-ID instructions and keep records.

claims.claim: Kraken Pro base tier (under $10K 30-day volume) charges 0.25% maker / 0.40% taker on spot; effective July 9, 2026 the fee tier is determined by 30-day spot volume OR assets on platform, whichever gives the better rate.
Kraken's cross-platform fee tier change (July 2026) is documented on its support site: tier now based on Spot volume or Assets on Platform, whichever qualifies you for the best rate.

Binance.US announced on April 22, 2026 spot trading fees of 0% maker / 0.02% taker on all pairs for every user, with no portfolio minimums, volume tiers, or subscription; marketed as up to 98% cheaper than Coinbase.
Binance.US's own blog states 0% maker / 0.02% taker spot fees; some third-party sources report 0% maker / 0.01% taker on core USD pairs, and a further 5% discount when fees are paid in BNB.

Coinbase Advanced base tier fees are reported inconsistently across 2026 sources: one set lists Intro 1 = 0.60% maker / 1.20% taker, Intro 2 (>=$1K) = 0.35% / 0.75%, Advanced 1 (>=$10K) = 0.25% / 0.40%, Advanced 2 (>=$50K) = 0.15% / 0.25%; others still show the older 0.40% maker / 0.60% taker entry level. The >=$10K tier at 0.25%/0.40% is the most consistent figure.

Coinbase lowered the qualifying 30-day volume threshold for Advanced fee tiers from $25,000 to $10,000 and allows instant VIP fee qualification via USDC holdings; the top VIP tier reaches 0 bps maker / 2 bps taker.

One 2026 summary reports Coinbase Advanced US entry-level fees of 0.50% maker / 0.90% taker (vs 0.25%/0.50% EU/UK); this conflicts with other sources and could not be verified against the blocked official fee page.

Coinbase simple (retail app) trades carry roughly a 0.50% spread markup in addition to fees; Coinbase One removes simple-trade fees but not the spread, and fee-free volume is capped at $500/month (Basic, $4.99) or $10,000/month (Preferred, $29.99), uncapped only on Premium ($299.99).

BTC-USD top-of-book bid-ask spreads on major US exchanges are typically well under 1 basis point (Kaiko cheatsheet: BTCUSD spreads often below 1 bp), so spread is negligible relative to exchange fees for a retail-size flip.

Kaiko research cited spreads falling to about 0.3 bps on Coinbase BTC-USD and 0.1 bps on Kraken (from >1 and 0.4 respectively), 1.9 bps on Bitstamp; the exact publication date of these figures was not confirmed.

Kaiko reported Binance.US has the widest spreads and worst liquidity among US venues for USD pairs, with BTC-USD real spreads approaching 3 bps at their worst; date of that observation not confirmed, so Binance.US's near-zero fees must be weighed against possibly thinner order books.

Fees, not signals, decide whether short-horizon crypto flipping is profitable: on a 0.1%/0.2% maker/taker venue a scalper doing ten round trips a day pays 2-4% in costs before any directional gain, and spot taker-both scalping can require ~90%+ win rates to break even on very small targets.

ARITHMETIC (computed from sourced fee levels, $7,500 position, 2.00% gross target): round-trip cost at Coinbase base tier taker-both (1.20% taker) = 2.40% = 120% of target (net loss); at 0.60% taker both legs = 1.20% RT (60% of target eaten); Kraken base or Coinbase >=$10K tier taker-both (0.40%) = 0.80% RT (40% eaten, net ~1.20%); maker-both at 0.25% = 0.50% RT (25% eaten, net ~1.50%); Binance.US 0.02% taker-both plus ~3 bps spread = ~0.07% RT (3% eaten, net ~1.93%).

ARITHMETIC (computed): with a symmetric +2% target / -2% stop, break-even win rate = (2% + RT cost)/4%: 0.80% RT needs 70% wins, 0.50% RT needs 62.5%, 0.04% RT needs 51%. At 55% win rate and 100 round trips/year on $7,500, expected pre-tax P&L is about -$4,500 at 0.80% RT, -$2,250 at 0.50% RT, and +$1,200 at 0.04% RT. A 1.5% target is only viable at sub-0.1% round-trip costs.

Short-term capital gains (crypto held one year or less) are taxed as ordinary income at 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37%; the 2026 rates are unchanged but bracket thresholds were inflation-adjusted upward.

The 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax applies to crypto gains (including short-term) when MAGI exceeds $200,000 (single/HoH), $250,000 (MFJ), $125,000 (MFS); thresholds are not inflation-indexed; top combined short-term rate is 40.8%.

As of 2026 the wash-sale rule (IRC Section 1091) does not apply to cryptocurrency because it is treated as property, not securities; a loss can be realized and the same asset repurchased immediately without disallowance.

H.R. 9172, the Applying Existing Tax Anti-Abuse Rules to Digital Assets Act (Rep. Arrington), was introduced June 8, 2026 and referred to House Ways and Means; it would apply wash-sale and constructive-sale rules to digital assets, excluding qualified USD stablecoins; as drafted the wash-sale change applies to dispositions after the introduction date, and JCT scored the wash-sale provision at about $2.074B over FY2026-2036.

On September 16, 2026 the House Ways and Means Committee advanced H.R. 10357, the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, by a 38-5 vote; it extends wash-sale, constructive-sale and other traditional rules to digital assets, adds a $10-or-less network-fee non-recognition rule for dispositions after Dec 31, 2027, and dropped the mining/staking deferral. It has not passed the full House or Senate and is not law.
The Ways and Means markup of H.R. 10357 (with H.R. 10334, 6130, 5439, 4093, 10346, 10356) is listed on the committee's official event page.

Form 1099-DA: brokers (exchanges, hosted wallets, payment processors) report gross proceeds for digital-asset sales beginning with 2025 transactions; cost-basis reporting is required only for 'covered' assets acquired on or after January 1, 2026 and held continuously at the same broker, with those forms arriving in early 2027; taxpayers remain responsible for determining basis and gain/loss.

IRS final regulations on broker digital-asset reporting and related guidance (including Notices 2024-56, 2025-7 and Rev. Proc. 2024-28) are consolidated on the IRS newsroom page; brokers were not required to report basis for 2025 sales.

Since January 1, 2025 taxpayers must track digital-asset cost basis wallet-by-wallet and account-by-account under Treas. Reg. 1.1012-1(j); FIFO is the default method unless specific identification (or a pre-sale standing instruction) is made; Rev. Proc. 2024-28 offered a one-time safe harbor to allocate pre-2025 unused basis across wallets, and taxpayers who missed it are locked into the allocation that existed on Jan 1, 2025.
Per-wallet rules explained: FIFO applies by default within each account; specific ID must be made no later than the time of sale; universal (cross-wallet) pooling is no longer allowed.

IRS Notice 2026-20 (issued March 17, 2026) extends the Notice 2025-7 temporary relief through December 31, 2026: taxpayers may satisfy specific identification for broker-held digital assets through their own books and records rather than instructing the broker, and may use FIFO for custodial accounts without penalty; for 2026 the basis a broker reports on 1099-DA may not match the taxpayer's own identification, and the taxpayer's records control but must be documented.

Practical consequence (inference from the FIFO-default and per-account rules): if the $5-10K flip pool is held in the same exchange account as the $70K long-term BTC, each flip sale will by default dispose of the oldest, typically lowest-basis long-term lots, realizing large taxable gains and eroding the long-term position; the flip pool should be isolated in a separate account/sub-account or covered by documented specific-ID instructions.
The 2026 filing season is described as a 'watershed' for crypto because it is the first with 1099-DA gross-proceeds reporting, increasing IRS matching of exchange-reported sales to returns.

research:paper-trading-platforms.summary: Research sweep on Bitcoin paper-trading platforms (2026), constrained by a blocked egress proxy and an exhausted WebSearch budget (only 2 of the planned 6+ searches ran; all vendor/review domains were blocked). Findings therefore lean on primary source files read from raw.githubusercontent.com and PyPI (official API-doc repos, SDK source, ccxt exchange classes), plus the two search summaries. What the evidence supports: (1) The three open-source bots differ sharply. Freqtrade dry-run is the most complete free, API-driven simulator: default-on, no exchange keys needed, simulates fills from the live order book (market orders max 5% slippage; limit orders fill when price is reached), persists trades to SQLite, and supports Kraken, binanceus, OKX, Bybit, etc. Hummingbot paper-trade simulates against live order books for Binance, KuCoin, Kraken and Gate.io with no API keys, with editable virtual balances; Apache-2.0, released 2026-09-05. Jesse (v3.2.0, 2026-09-17) supports paper trading, but its own info.py marks live/paper on Coinbase Spot, Kraken Spot, Binance and Bybit as requiring a 'premium' plan; only testnets and custom data are 'free'. (2) Exchange-hosted demos vary in realism. Coinbase Advanced Trade sandbox returns mocked responses for only Accounts/Orders endpoints, so it cannot score a strategy; Coinbase Exchange has a separate sandbox host (api-public.sandbox.exchange.coinbase.com) whose data realism is unverified. Kraken spot has no sandbox (ccxt sandbox: False); Kraken Futures has a demo at demo-futures.kraken.com. Binance's Spot Testnet has prices and order books independent from the live exchange (bad for scoring), whereas Binance's newer Demo Mode (demo-api.binance.com) mirrors live prices but needs a Binance.com login and Binance itself warns realistic != real. Bybit demo (api-demo.bybit.com) uses live markets, funds on request, keeps orders only 7 days; OKX demo is the production host plus an 'x-simulated-trading: 1' header. (3) Alpaca paper trading is free, default-on in alpaca-py (paper=True -> paper-api.alpaca.markets), uses separate paper keys, supports crypto with tiered fees and unauthenticated crypto data, but paper hosts do not serve the crypto wallets API; state availability and fill mechanics were not verifiable. (4) TradingView paper trading (per search summaries only): free on Basic, crypto data real-time, $100k resettable balance, market/limit/stop/bracket orders; no public API for paper orders was found. (5) 3Commas, Cryptohopper and Pionex could not be verified at all (all domains blocked). Recommendations, non-programmer: TradingView paper trading (GUI, free, real-time crypto), Alpaca paper account (US broker with crypto and a web dashboard), and, if eligible, Bybit demo or Binance Demo Mode; API-driven agent: Freqtrade dry-run on Kraken/binanceus (best fit for the planned Python paper sim and scoring), Hummingbot paper-trade (Kraken/Binance live books, no keys), and Alpaca paper API (real US broker semantics, separate keys). Avoid the Coinbase Advanced sandbox and Binance Spot Testnet for performance scoring.

claims.claim: Freqtrade dry-run mode is on by default (dry_run defaults to true) and the simulated wallet defaults to 1000 stake-currency units (dry_run_wallet), settable as a float or per-asset dict.

In Freqtrade dry-run, market orders 'fill based on orderbook volume the moment the order is placed, with a maximum slippage of 5%'; limit orders 'fill once the price reaches the defined level' or time out per unfilledtimeout; limit orders crossing price by >1% convert to market orders; stoploss_on_exchange is assumed filled.

Freqtrade dry-run persists trades to SQLite (db_url defaults to sqlite:///tradesv3.dryrun.sqlite when dry_run is true) and does not require exchange API keys ('API-keys may or may not be provided. Only Read-Only operations ... are performed in dry-run mode').
Freqtrade supports Binance, Kraken, OKX, Gate, Bybit and others for spot, has a builtin WebUI and Telegram control, and its README says 'Always start by running a trading bot in Dry-Run'.

Freqtrade docs: US users must use the ccxt exchange id 'binanceus' rather than 'binance'; Kraken's API only provides 720 historic candles, 'sufficient for Freqtrade dry-run and live trade modes, but is a problem for backtesting'; Kraken supports stoploss_on_exchange.

Freqtrade docs describe Bybit demo mode (exchange.demo_trading=true) as using 'live markets to simulate your trades (without market impact) - making it work very similar to freqtrade's dry-run mode'; it needs separate demo API keys and 'Demo mode is incompatible with dry-run.'

Hummingbot paper trade lets users 'simulate trading strategies without risking any actual assets'; by default paper trade is enabled for Binance, KuCoin, Kraken and Gate.io (connector names like kraken_paper_trade), and exchange APIs are not required for pure/cross-exchange/Avellaneda market making in paper mode.

Hummingbot paper accounts start with BTC 1, USDT 100000, USDC 100000, ETH 20, WETH 20, SOL 100, DOGE 1000000, HBOT 10000000, adjustable via 'balance paper [asset] [amount]' or conf_client.yml paper_trade.paper_trade_account_balance.
Hummingbot's README says paper trading 'simulates trading against live Binance market data, so no API keys are required', and the project is 'open source and licensed under Apache 2.0'.

Hummingbot's paper-trade connector fills market orders by walking the live order book (order_book.simulate_buy / simulate_sell) and applies estimated trade fees via build_trade_fee before emitting OrderFilledEvents.
Hummingbot's latest PyPI release is version 20260901, released 2026-09-05, requiring Python >=3.10.12.

Jesse supports paper trading as a live-session mode ('Supports paper trading, multiple accounts, real-time logs & notifications'; enums define live_session_modes LIVETRADE and PAPERTRADE) and its latest PyPI release is 3.2.0 on 2026-09-17.

Jesse's own exchange registry (jesse/info.py) marks 'required_live_plan': 'premium' for Coinbase Spot, Kraken Pro Spot, Binance Spot, Bybit and KuCoin (33 entries); only 5 entries are 'free' (Apex, Hyperliquid, Lighter and Kraken Pro Futures testnets, plus custom data), so live/paper trading on the user's real exchanges is gated behind a paid plan.

Jesse's registry sets backtesting False for Kraken Pro Spot because Kraken's public OHLC endpoint only serves the most recent 720 candles, and lists representative fees of 0.0003 for Coinbase Spot and 0.0026 for Kraken Spot (noting the real Kraken fee depends on volume tier).

Alpaca's official SDK TradingClient defaults to paper=True and routes to BaseURL.TRADING_PAPER = https://paper-api.alpaca.markets (live is https://api.alpaca.markets); the docstring says to 'Use paper keys if paper is set to true'.

Alpaca docs in the SDK repo: 'Alpaca offers a paper trading sandbox environment so you can test out the API or paper trade your strategy before you go live'; keys must 'correspond to a paper account'; crypto is tradable via the same API and 'crypto trading fees are tiered'; notional orders work for any crypto order type.
Alpaca crypto market data (CryptoHistoricalDataClient / CryptoDataStream) needs 'no keys required for crypto data'.
ccxt's alpaca connector notes that 'paper-trading hosts do not serve the crypto wallets api at all', a known limitation of Alpaca paper mode for crypto.

Coinbase Advanced Trade API sandbox (https://api-sandbox.coinbase.com/api/v3/brokerage/{resource}) exposes only Accounts and Orders endpoints, and 'All responses are mocked but have the same format as production' (an X-Sandbox header triggers predefined variance) — it is not a live-price simulation.

ccxt's 'coinbase' (Advanced Trade) class declares sandbox: False and defines no test URLs, while the separate 'coinbaseexchange' class has a sandbox at https://api-public.sandbox.exchange.coinbase.com.

Kraken spot has no sandbox (ccxt kraken class: 'sandbox': False), whereas Kraken Futures has a demo environment at https://demo-futures.kraken.com/derivatives/api/ (ccxt krakenfutures test URLs, sandbox: True).

Binance Spot Testnet base endpoint is https://testnet.binance.vision/api; 'API keys can be created on the SPOT Test Network upon logging in with your Github account'; the testnet is 'only available via the API' and supports only /api/* endpoints.

Binance's own comparison: Spot Testnet 'prices and order books are independent from the live exchange' and balances reset monthly; Spot Demo Mode (REST https://demo-api.binance.com/api, created after logging into a Binance account) has prices and order books 'similar to the live exchange', user-resettable balances, and identical limits — with the warning 'Realistic market data is not equal to real market data. Do not assume trading strategies that work in Demo Mode will work in the live exchange.'

Bybit demo trading uses REST https://api-demo.bybit.com and WS wss://stream-demo.bybit.com, demo funds are requested via POST /v5/account/demo-apply-money, all Market endpoints plus order/position/account endpoints are available, but 'Orders generated in demo trading keep 7 days', rate limits are 'Default rate limit, not upgradable', and the demo account is an independent UID that 'does not have a complete function compared with the real trading service'.

Bybit's official pybit SDK selects api-testnet vs api-demo subdomains via testnet=True / demo=True flags; ccxt likewise exposes api-testnet.bybit.com and api-demo.bybit.com with an enableDemoTrading option.

OKX demo trading runs on the production host with the header 'x-simulated-trading: 1' (python-okx flag='1' vs '0'; ccxt set_sandbox_mode adds the same header), so demo orders are simulated against the live OKX market rather than a separate testnet.
OKX's official Python SDK: 'Tweak the value of the parameter flag (live trading: 0, demo trading: 1) to switch between live and demo trading environment'.

ccxt unifies sandbox access via exchange.set_sandbox_mode(True), which must be the first call after creating the exchange; sandbox keys come from registering on the exchange's sandbox site and 'Sandbox keys are not interchangeable with production keys!'
TradingView: cryptocurrency exchange feeds are real-time for every user including the free plan ('Crypto is always real-time for every user, direct from the exchange').

TradingView paper trading is available on every plan including free Basic with no credit card, uses real-time market data, starts with a $100,000 virtual balance that can be reset from the Trading Panel, and supports market, limit, stop, stop-limit and bracket orders across many symbols.
TradingView's official support article 'Paper trading — main functionality' exists and documents the simulator; no public API for placing paper-trading orders was found in any result (not found).
