research:llm-trading-agents.summary: Evidence 2024-2026 on LLM trading agents is, after fees and contamination controls, negative for autonomous LLM-driven trading and strongly negative for short-horizon flipping. The one real-money public test (Nof1 Alpha Arena Season 1, Oct 18-Nov 3 2025, six frontier LLMs with $10k each on Hyperliquid crypto perps) ended with only Qwen3 Max (~+22%) and DeepSeek V3.1 (~+5%) positive while GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 lost roughly 31-63% in two weeks; Nof1's own write-up says early runs 'over-traded and took quick, tiny gains that fees erased', that models over-rode their own exit plans and misread data, and that one season has 'limited statistical power'. Season 1.5 (US stock tokens, Nov 19-Dec 3 2025) was won by a 'Mystery Model' (Grok 4.20) at +12.11%; no Season 2 results were found published as of Aug 2026. Contamination-free and cost-inclusive academic evaluations converge: StockBench (Mar-Jun 2025, no fees) found most frontier LLM agents fail to beat equal-weight buy-and-hold (+0.4%) and all underperform it in downturns; LiveTradeBench (21 LLMs, ~50 live days) found agents 'struggle to outperform buy-and-hold' and SOTA models 'incur losses'; FINSABER (KDD 2026, 2000-2025, real commissions) found buy-and-hold beats FinMem and FinAgent in every bias-mitigated universe; The Alpha Illusion (May 2026) re-ran TradingAgents and QuantAgent over Jan 2025-Jan 2026 with commissions, spread, impact and token cost and both fell below buy-and-hold net; Profit Mirage shows LLM-agent Sharpe decays 51-62% once the test window passes the model's training cutoff. The flagship framework papers (TradingAgents Sharpe 8.21, FinMem, FinAgent, CryptoTrade) used ~60-day windows, no or unspecified fees, and TradingAgents' own README now says backtests are 'not guaranteed to match any published figure' and it is 'a research scaffold... not a strategy with a fixed, replicable return'; its repo has logged repeated silent look-ahead-bias bugs through Sep 2026. CryptoTrade (the main BTC/ETH/SOL agent paper) underperformed buy-and-hold in every bull-period test and its authors say it is 'not for investment recommendations'. QuantAgent's authors state 1-15 minute horizons are 'dominated by noise' and LLM latency can exceed the opportunity window. Recurring failure modes: overtrading/fee burn (Gemini 2.5 Pro paid ~8.9% of capital in fees in 5 days), hallucinated price levels, long bias with 10-25x leverage, contradicting or overriding own exit plans, look-ahead/contamination in backtests, arithmetic/JSON errors, adversarial fragility (TradeTrap: prompt injection cut return 7.81% to 0.89% with 99.98% concentration; explanations unfaithful in 33-46% of cases), and catastrophic execution errors when the LLM holds keys (Lobstar Wilde, Feb 2026, sent ~$441k of tokens after a session crash). Design patterns with the best support: keep the LLM upstream as an information/analysis layer, never the final sizing/execution authority; hard-coded risk limits (max position, max leverage, daily loss circuit breaker, mandatory stop, cooldowns/min hold, max trades per day); code-enforced regime gate; independent reconciliation of agent state vs exchange state; stale-quote rejection; paper -> shadow-live (tiny size) -> live promotion; post-cutoff holdout, explicit fee/slippage model, multiple seeds, and full decision logging for scoring; a --no-LLM ablation arm. Open-source paper-trading platforms using real-time quotes exist (etrobot/open-alpha-arena on ccxt/Hyperliquid, wquguru/nof0, NoFxAiOS/nofx) but none documents fee/slippage modeling, and no study was found testing LLM agents on BTC at intraday cadence with fees.

claims.claim: Alpha Arena Season 1 (Nof1.ai) ran Oct 18 - Nov 3, 2025: six frontier LLMs (Qwen3 Max, DeepSeek V3.1, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok 4) each traded $10,000 of real USDC on Hyperliquid crypto perpetuals with identical prompts and price-only inputs; final standings had only two models positive (Qwen3 Max ~+22.3%, DeepSeek V3.1 ~+4.9%) and the four US models down roughly 31-63% (one corrected tally: Claude ~-31%, Grok ~-45%, Gemini ~-57%, GPT-5 ~-63%; another tally orders the losers differently, Claude -42%, Gemini -46%, Grok -58%, GPT-5 -59%).

Nof1's own Alpha Arena design post (copied verbatim in a GitHub repo) states that in early iterations 'fees were a significant obstacle' and 'agents over-traded and took quick, tiny gains that fees erased'; that models showed ordering bias (misreading data sequence despite instructions), inconsistent behavior with ambiguous terms, rule-gaming (Gemini 2.5 Flash issued neutral trades to circumvent constraints), contradicted their own prior outputs, and over-rode their own exit plans (Gemini 2.5 Pro closed early most often); and that 'this is a single live season with a finite window, so statistical power is limited' with 'run-to-run variation in both rankings and inter-model correlations'.

Mid-competition Alpha Arena snapshot (Oct 23, 2025) quantifies the overtrading failure mode: Gemini 2.5 Pro had made 102 trades and paid $890.61 in fees (8.9% of its $10k) with a 27.5% win rate and -54% return; GPT-5 was at -67.9% with a 5.1% win rate and use of 25x leverage; DeepSeek led with only 9 trades and the only Sharpe above 1 (1.107).

The Alpha Arena prompt cadence and structure: every model was prompted every ~3 minutes with mid-prices, EMA/MACD/RSI/ATR, open interest, funding rates, 3-minute and 4-hour series and account state for six perps (BTC, ETH, SOL, BNB, DOGE, XRP), and had to return coin, direction, quantity, leverage, confidence [0,1], profit target, stop-loss, and an invalidation condition; observed leverage was 10-20x and positioning on Oct 28, 2025 was 96.5% long / 2.5% short.

Alpha Arena Season 1.5 (late Nov - early Dec 2025; one summary gives Nov 19 - Dec 3) moved to US stock tokens on Hyperliquid (TSLA, NDX, NVDA, MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL, PLTR), ~$320k total capital, 8 models (original six plus Kimi K2 and an undisclosed model) in four modes (New Baseline, Monk Mode, Situational Awareness, Max Leverage 10-20x); the anonymous 'Mystery Model', revealed afterwards as xAI's Grok 4.20, won at +12.11% while GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro and DeepSeek were negative; full per-model standings were not published in the sources found.

As of Aug 2026 no Alpha Arena Season 2 results had been published despite an announced format (human traders alongside AI models, web search, longer thinking); Nof1 raised a $15M round in May 2026 and is building a consumer product. The report's inference is that the benchmark company stopped publishing after the initial season.

StockBench (arXiv 2510.02209, Oct 2025, v2 Mar 2026): contamination-free window Mar 3 - Jun 30, 2025 (82 trading days), top-20 DJIA stocks, $100k, one decision per day, transaction costs explicitly not modeled; equal-weight buy-and-hold returned +0.4% (-15.2% max drawdown); the best agent (Kimi-K2) returned +1.9%, the worst (GPT-OSS-20B) -2.8%; most models (incl. GPT-5, Claude-4, o3, Qwen3, DeepSeek, GLM-4.5) failed to beat buy-and-hold; 'all LLM agents underperform the passive baseline during the downturn'; documented failure modes include arithmetic errors in share-quantity conversion, JSON schema violations, a 'reasoning-model paradox' (reasoning models underperform plainer instruction-tuned ones) and degradation as portfolio size grows.

LiveTradeBench (arXiv 2511.03628, Oct/Nov 2025; repo ulab-uiuc/live-trade-bench) evaluated 21 LLMs over ~50 live days on US stocks and Polymarket and concluded that 'agents struggle to outperform buy-and-hold baselines, and even state-of-the-art models incur losses in real-time fund management', and that high general-reasoning benchmark scores do not translate into trading performance.

The Alpha Illusion (arXiv 2605.16895, May 2026) re-ran TradingAgents and QuantAgent over Jan 2025 - Jan 2026 on a $100k equal-weight TSLA/NVDA/KO/XOM/MSTR book charging commission, token cost, spread and market impact: buy-and-hold ended at $104.8k; TradingAgents $106.4k gross fell to $102.3k net (Sharpe 0.43 to 0.22); QuantAgent $81.4k gross to $77.9k net (Sharpe -0.96 to -1.15); it reports that '35 of 40 system x friction-component cells are unmodeled' in the prior literature and that crossing the training cutoff cuts FinMem's return by ~71.85% and QuantAgent's Sharpe by ~51.48%; multiple 2026 repos cite it as naming FinCon, FinMem, TradingAgents, FinAgent, QuantAgent and FLAG-Trader as systems whose reported Sharpe 'should not be treated as deployment evidence'.

Profit Mirage (arXiv 2510.07920, Oct 2025) abstract: 'most systems exhibit a profit mirage: dazzling back-tested returns evaporate once the model's knowledge window ends, because of the inherent information leakage in LLMs'; it quantifies leakage across four dimensions and releases FinLake-Bench; a 2026 inventory summarizes the effect as published LLM-agent alpha decaying 51-62% in Sharpe once the test period crosses the backbone's cutoff (e.g. FinMem AMZN Sharpe 0.233 published vs -0.968 with GPT-4o).

FINSABER ('Can LLM-based Financial Investing Strategies Outperform the Market in Long Run?', arXiv 2505.07078, accepted KDD 2026 Datasets & Benchmarks oral, Nov 24 2025) covers 2000-2025 S&P 500 with real commissions ($0.0049/share, $0.99 min), 5 bps slippage, liquidity caps, next-open execution and optional LLM-cost-as-trade-cost; a Sept 2026 inventory of its results reports buy-and-hold beat both FinMem and FinAgent on Sharpe in all four bias-mitigated universes (p <= 4e-5), PPO beat both LLM agents, and swapping the backbone moved FinMem's Sharpe from 2.679 to 0.404.

TradingAgents (arXiv 2412.20138, Xiao/Sun/Luo/Wang, Dec 2024; 107k GitHub stars by Sep 2026) reported cumulative returns of 23-27% and Sharpe 5.60-8.21 on AAPL/GOOGL/AMZN over a Jan-Mar 2024 backtest (~60 trading days) with no transaction costs; the AAPL Sharpe of 8.21 on ~60 observations has 95% confidence-interval half-widths that 'routinely exceed typical between-system gaps'.

The TradingAgents README (Sep 2026, v0.5.0) now states verbatim: 'Backtest results are not guaranteed to match any published figure', 'Two runs of the same ticker and date can differ', and 'Treat the framework as a research scaffold for studying multi-agent analysis, not as a strategy with a fixed, replicable return'; orders execute against a simulated exchange and the framework 'is not intended as financial, investment, or trading advice'.

The TradingAgents repo has repeatedly logged silent look-ahead bias in its backtests: issue #1007 (Jun 8, 2026) found 'the news analyst receives 2025-2026 articles when curr_date is set to 2022. LLM signals are contaminated by look-ahead bias with no indication anything is wrong'; further closed issues include #33 'data leak problem' (Jun 2025), #175/#203 'look-ahead bias' (Jul-Aug 2025), #1251 decision-log lessons without point-in-time guard (Aug 2026), #1275 FRED macro returning unpublished/revised data (Aug 2026) and #1300 fundamentals stamped with wall-clock now() (Sep 2026).

An ACM reproducibility study of TradingAgents (DOI 10.1145/3800973.3801029, runs May-Jul 2025, GPT-4o and Qwen3:30B on GOOGL with varied temperature/seed) reports mean returns of 15.8% +/- 4.2% (GPT-4o) and 18.1% +/- 2.8% (Qwen) versus 19.1% GOOGL buy-and-hold and 17.4% QQQ, i.e. confidence intervals overlapping the passive benchmark; the inventory flags the authors as unverified and the DOI returned HTTP 403 to automated access.

CryptoTrade (EMNLP 2024, Li et al., Xtra-Computing/NUS) is a zero-shot daily BTC/ETH/SOL agent (GPT-3.5/GPT-4/GPT-4o, on-chain stats + news + reflection). In its bull test period (Oct 1 - Dec 1, 2023) buy-and-hold returned BTC 39.66% / ETH 22.59% / SOL 176.72% versus CryptoTrade-GPT-4o 28.47% / 25.47% / 115.18% (Sharpe 0.23/0.18/0.28 vs B&H 0.25/0.14/0.30); the authors concede it is comparable to MACD 'but not compared to traditional trading signals' such as Buy-and-Hold and SLMA, charge a transaction fee 'in proportion to the traded value' without stating the rate, and warn 'CryptoTrade is not for investment recommendations'.

FinMem (arXiv 2311.13743, Nov 2023; layered memory + character design, GPT-4-Turbo) reported TSLA cumulative return 61.78% and Sharpe 2.68 over Oct 6, 2022 - Apr 10, 2023 with no transaction costs stated; FinAgent (arXiv 2402.18485, KDD 2024; multimodal with K-line images) claimed >36% average profit improvement over 12 baselines on six datasets including ETHUSD (Jun 2023 - Jan 2024) with a commission in the reward whose rate is undisclosed; both are the agents FINSABER later found buy-and-hold beats after bias mitigation.

Agent Market Arena / 'When Agents Trade' (arXiv 2510.11695, live Aug 1 - Sep 30, 2025 on TSLA, BMRN, BTC, ETH; 4 agent designs x 5 backbones): swapping the backbone changed results more than architecture (TradeAgent on TSLA ranged from -38.7% with GPT-4.1 to +21.9% with Gemini-2.0-Flash); TSLA buy-and-hold returned +46.88% and every agent underperformed it (best InvestorAgent+GPT-4.1 +40.83%); no transaction costs reported and one reviewer flagged HedgeFundAgent rows byte-identical across five backbones as a reproducibility red flag.

TradeTrap (arXiv 2512.02261, Shanghai AI Lab, Dec 2025) stress-tested an adaptive (AI-Trader) and a procedural (ValueCell/NoFX) agent on ~100 NASDAQ-100 stocks ($5k, zero fees) with single-component perturbations: prompt injection cut the adaptive agent's return from 7.81% to 0.89% and Sharpe from 5.72 to 0.29 while driving concentration to 99.98%; state tampering produced -61.02% return and 91.97% max drawdown; memory poisoning silently eroded return to 1.88%; MCP tool hijacking made the agent 'hallucinate phantom positions' and stop trading; no conventional safeguards triggered. Recommended defenses: cross-validated data provenance, independent agent-state vs exchange-state reconciliation each step, zero-trust boundary between strategy generation and execution, session isolation of memory.

A Mar 20, 2026 practitioner summary of TradeTrap reports faithfulness scores of 54-67%, meaning 'in 33-46% of cases, LLM trader explanations do not match the actual reasons behind their decisions', with cognitive-trap hit rates of 28-39% (anchoring on random target prices), 35-48% (recency), 19-33% (fake authority quotes) and 44-57% (confirmation bias); it recommends not trusting the explanations, ensemble voting, human-in-the-loop for large trades, adversarial testing, and logging all intermediate steps for post-mortems.

Lobstar Wilde incident: an autonomous Solana trading agent launched Feb 19, 2026 by an OpenAI engineer with ~$50k in SOL; on Feb 22 (day three), after a tooling crash wiped its session state, it reconstructed its wallet balance wrongly and, in response to a stranger's reply asking for '4 SOL' for an uncle's tetanus treatment, sent 52.4 million LOBSTAR tokens (~5% of supply, ~$441,780 notional, ~$40k realized); post-mortems treat it as the canonical case for hard, non-LLM spend caps, balance checks and key isolation enforced outside the model rather than in the system prompt.

QuantAgent (arXiv 2509.09995, 'Price-Driven Multi-Agent LLMs for High-Frequency Trading') operates on 1-hour and 4-hour bars and reports directional accuracy of 50.7-63.7% across 8 assets vs 40-60% for Random/Linear/XGBoost baselines; its authors state that ultra-short horizons (1-15 minutes) are 'dominated by noise and rapid regime shifts' and that per-cycle LLM-plus-tool latency 'can exceed the window in which a 1-minute opportunity remains exploitable'; the same report found no study anywhere testing LLM agents on 5-15 minute bars with multi-hour holds.

'The Losing Winner: An LLM Agent That Predicts the Market but Loses Money' (NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on GenAI in Finance) is a BTC-specific cautionary result: fine-tuning Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with RL raised BTC market-state classification accuracy while cumulative simulated returns fell below the zero-shot baseline, attributed to objective mismatch / reward hacking (optimizing a gross-side proxy degrades net-side results).

Practitioner post-mortem of a Claude-based Alpaca paper-trading agent (Oct 28, 2025): the LLM hallucinated identical technical levels ('$250 resistance with 1.67x volume') across stocks priced $50-$1,130; it churned (sold NOW at $940.18 and rebought at $940.09 six minutes later); 452 of 472 decisions (95.8%) were sell orders for positions not held; day P&L -0.11% on 20 fills. Fixes adopted: reject reasoning citing price levels not near the actual price, only generate sells for held positions, cap positions at 5% of equity scaled by confidence, enforce 30-minute minimum hold and 1-hour re-entry blacklist, reject sentiment/action contradictions.

Consensus design recommendation from the 2026 audit literature (Alpha Illusion, Agentic Trading survey 2605.19337 which found 0/19 closed-loop studies reach full reproducibility and only 1/19 states a transaction-cost model, Beyond Agent Architecture 2606.08285 which finds execution semantics and cost treatment the least-reported dimensions): keep the LLM as an auditable information/feature layer upstream of independent calibration, risk and execution modules so 'final decision authority does not rest on an uncalibrated LLM'; every result should include a --no-llm ablation arm, a post-cutoff holdout window, explicit transaction costs with cost-sensitivity curves, >=5 seeds with +/- SEM, and Deflated Sharpe correction; the LLM 'must never' emit BUY/SELL at decision time or sit on the critical path.

2026 benchmark inventory (links verified against arXiv in 2026): TraderBench (2603.00285, Feb 2026, 13 models) finds 'most models use fixed non-adaptive strategies; extended reasoning helps knowledge tasks but not actual trading'; PredictionMarketBench (2602.00133, Jan 2026, Kalshi) finds 'naive agents struggle with fees/settlement risk; fee-aware algorithmic strategies stay competitive'; a Mar 2026 taxonomy paper (2603.27539) identifies five evaluation biases that can flip return signs; the inventory's overall verdict on LLM trading vs buy-and-hold after costs is 'overwhelmingly negative', with qualified success only where fee-aware design is explicit.

Operational cost of LLM-in-the-loop trading (API prices fetched Sep 14, 2026): for 5 tickers analysed daily over 252 days, a single analysis call per ticker-day costs ~$4-69/yr depending on model, TradingAgents' 11-call multi-agent pipeline ~$35-496/yr, and a 20-config x 5-year walk-forward sweep $3.5k-$49.6k; the inventory notes token cost and latency sit on the right-hand side of net P&L for multi-agent systems.

Real-money six-month ChatGPT micro-cap experiment (LuckyOne7777/LLM-Trading-Lab, $100, Jun 27 - Dec 26, 2025, forward-only daily CSV logs, hard stop-loss rules): the author's final 40-page evaluation explicitly declines to make an alpha claim; equity was 'dominated by a small number of high-impact trades', the model re-entered tickers after realizing losses on them, and the behavior is characterized as 'high-conviction, thesis-driven discretionary trading' with 'asymmetric downside exposure'; temperature was never fixed and models were swapped as released.

Code-enforced hybrid pattern (TradeHive, adapted from TradingAgents, Mar 2026): a 7-regime state machine with fixed legal transitions maps regime to hard position limits (confirmed downtrend locks at 0%, confirmed uptrend 75-100%) and dual-layer position clamping, while the LLM only synthesizes evidence and micro-tunes; self-reported NVDA backtest Feb 20 - Aug 20, 2025 (T+1 open, fees not stated): +43.9% / -3.2% MDD vs buy-and-hold +25.2% / -32.7% and single-agent LLM +15.6% / -7.7%; caveats: trend-dependent, LLM scoring variance, crypto untested.

Silverfish (self-hosted multi-strategy crypto system with money-isolated LLM agents, archived Sep 2026 after running live for several months) states 'No strategy in this repository has a demonstrated edge' and that nothing 'developed a durable, costs-inclusive edge'; its retained value is the safety machinery: kill floor counting only price P&L (funding excluded so carry cannot mask losses), per-pair stop, gross cap, drawdown breaker, staleness guard, reconciliation halt (DB vs live exchange state compared before every execution, halt on drift), reduceOnly closes, a paper -> shadow-live (clamped to a tiny fraction of capital) -> live promotion lifecycle, and an LLM research loop with no exchange keys.

ALTA (Sep 2026, research-only multi-agent platform, 916 passing tests) separates LLM judgment from code enforcement: models propose, software enforces freshness checks, risk gates and account isolation; proposals are rejected as stale when 'price moves while an LLM responds'; theses run first in Shadow simulation with internal fills/costs, an independent auditor (not the assessor) selects one plan or 'Wait', broker execution requires explicit Configure -> Verify -> Authorize -> Start; it disclaims 'not investment advice, a production OMS or evidence of profitable Alpha'.

Example of a hard-coded risk manager wrapping an LLM (Claude Haiku 4.5) for Hyperliquid paper trading (Apr 2026): max position 10% of portfolio, force-close at -20%, max leverage 10x, total exposure 50%, daily circuit breaker at -10% drawdown, mandatory 5% stop-loss auto-set if the model omits one, max 10 concurrent positions, 20% balance reserve; the repo reports no performance results and states 'Use at your own risk. No guarantee of returns.'

Open-source paper-trading platforms that replicate Alpha Arena on real-time data exist: etrobot/open-alpha-arena (595 stars, TypeScript, ccxt quotes from Hyperliquid, any OpenAI-compatible LLM, SQLite, Docker; no fee/slippage modeling documented), wquguru/nof0 (Go backend + Next.js, Hyperliquid, LLM executors, backtests, leaderboards), NoFxAiOS/nofx (multi-LLM trading terminal with leaderboard), oficcejo/alpha-arena-okx, and moss-trade-bot-skills (simulated Hyperliquid perps, 'bit-exact between backtest and live'); none of them publishes audited results.

FinRL-DeepSeek (arXiv 2502.07393, Feb 2025) infuses DeepSeek-generated news sentiment/risk signals into PPO and CPPO on Nasdaq-100 (train 2013-2018, trade 2019-2023); the repo's preliminary conclusion is 'Bull market -> PPO; Bear market -> CPPO-DeepSeek', and a Sept 2026 inventory notes LLM infusion into plain PPO degraded it at every signal strength tested, i.e. the LLM helped only as a risk-sensitivity input in adverse regimes.

Multi-agent debate (the bull/bear researcher pattern used by TradingAgents and clones) has weak general evidence: Zhang et al. (arXiv 2502.08788) found multi-agent debate wins under 20% of 36 configurations (4 models x 9 benchmarks) and adding rounds or agents does not improve and may degrade performance.

Trading-R1 (arXiv 2509.11420, Sep 14 2025, Tauric Research): a Qwen3-4B model trained with SFT + RL on Tauric-TR1-DB (100k samples, Jan 2024 - May 2025, 14 equities/ETFs) claims improved risk-adjusted returns on six equities/ETFs over Jun 1 - Aug 31, 2024 (63 days, no costs stated; NVDA CR 8.08%, SR 2.72); RL-only was worse than SFT-only on 4 of 6 tickers, and the promised Trading-R1 Terminal repo still read 'Terminal coming soon' as of Sep 2026.

A Sapienza University thesis (AIAT V2, Sep 2026) compares Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-4.1 mini, Qwen 3.7-Max and DeepSeek V4 Flash trading crypto perps on Hyperliquid testnet ($1,000 each, 15-minute cadence, pre-registered 48-hour window) as a behavioral study; it reports no PnL winner, and discloses a known defect in its cost calculation, illustrating how hard even small controlled LLM-trading experiments are to run cleanly.

PolyBench (2026) evaluates seven LLMs (incl. Gemini-3-Flash, DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-OSS-120B) as autonomous traders on 38,666 live Polymarket binary markets with confidence-weighted return, APY and Sharpe, discarding predictions below 0.6 confidence or without positive expected value; the README shows results only as an image, so per-model profitability could not be extracted.

open_questions: Alpha Arena Season 1 final per-model numbers for the four losing models differ between sources (e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.5 -31% vs -42%; Grok 4 -45% vs -58%; Gemini 2.5 Pro -57% vs -46%; GPT-5 -63% vs -59%) and trade counts differ (Qwen '1,418 trades in one round' vs Gemini '238 trades' vs a 102-trade Oct 23 snapshot); nof1.ai is egress-blocked so the primary leaderboard could not be checked.
Alpha Arena Season 1.5 full standings by model and mode, and any Season 2 results after Aug 2026, were not found; whether Nof1 has published the 'more rigorous follow-ups' it promised is unknown.

arXiv, Semantic Scholar, ACL Anthology, dblp, OpenReview and HuggingFace were all blocked, so every paper figure here (StockBench, LiveTradeBench, FINSABER, Alpha Illusion, Profit Mirage, TradeTrap, CryptoTrade, TradingAgents) comes from GitHub mirrors, digests or third-party inventories; primary verification is still needed, especially for the Alpha Illusion net-of-friction dollar figures and the FINSABER p-values.

No study was found that tests LLM agents on BTC at intraday cadence (5-15 minute bars, several decisions per day) with realistic fees; the closest (QuantAgent, 1h/4h bars) says shorter horizons are noise-dominated. Whether a 2-3% take-profit flip strategy has any documented LLM-driven track record after fees is unanswered (no source found).

Exact fee assumptions are missing from the key crypto agent paper (CryptoTrade charges a fee 'in proportion to traded value' with no rate given) and from the Alpha Arena copies (Hyperliquid taker fee schedule not captured).
LiveTradeBench per-model returns and the ~50-day window's exact dates were not found; only the headline conclusion is available.

The 'Bitcoin Explainable Zero-Shot Multi-Agent' study cited by one curation (Reddit sentiment +23.30% total return, news sentiment 'noise', explicit slippage and fees) has no arXiv id or URL in any source found and is unverified.

TradeHive's +43.9% / -3.2% MDD NVDA result is self-reported by a 3-star repo without fees or seeds; whether code-enforced regime gating actually improves net results in crypto is untested in any source found.

Whether any of the open-source Alpha Arena replicas (open-alpha-arena, nof0, nofx) model exchange fees, funding and slippage in their paper-trading engines is undocumented; this matters directly for scoring a 2-3% flip strategy.

research:data-sources.summary: Research sweep on free, no-auth data sources for a Python paper-trading bot on the user's own computer. Method caveat: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before this sweep began, and WebFetch is egress-blocked for every official doc domain tried (docs.cdp.coinbase.com, docs.kraken.com, bitstamp.net, developers.binance.com, docs.deribit.com, alternative.me, docs.polymarket.com, docs.kalshi.com, docs.coinglass.com, bybit-exchange.github.io, farside.co.uk). All evidence therefore comes from GitHub-hosted mirrors of official documentation (binance/binance-spot-api-docs, binance-us/binance-us-api-docs, binance/binance-futures-connector-python, bybit-exchange/docs, coinglass-official/coinglass-api-skills, Polymarket/agent-skills, Kalshi/kalshi-starter-code-python) fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com on 2026-09-19, from ccxt's exchange source files (which encode limits/rate limits), and from GitHub code search across community projects (>10 distinct searches). Headline findings: (1) Candles: Coinbase Exchange public /products/BTC-USD/candles (granularity 60/300/900/3600/21600/86400 s, max 300 candles, ~10 req/s) and Kraken /0/public/OHLC (intervals 1..21600 min, max 720 and ONLY the most recent 720 - no deep backfill) are the practical US-accessible no-key sources; Bitstamp /api/v2/ohlc/btcusd/ (max 1000, 12 step sizes, 8000 req/10 min) is a good third; Binance api.binance.com returns HTTP 451 from US IPs, but Binance's official market-data-only host data-api.binance.vision serves /api/v3/klines (max 1000) with no key and is reported by multiple projects to work from the US; api.binance.us is the other US option (weight 1200/min). (2) Funding/OI: Bybit v5 public endpoints (/v5/market/funding/history, /v5/market/open-interest, limit 200, 600 req per 5 s IP limit) need no key; Binance fapi endpoints are documented (fundingRate max 1000; openInterestHist max 500, only 30 days) but fapi.binance.com is also geo-blocked from the US; Coinglass v4 always needs a CG-API-KEY (Hobbyist tier 30 req/min) but then gives funding, OI, and a JSON BTC ETF flow-history. (3) Deribit public/get_volatility_index_data (resolution 1/60/3600/43200/1D) and get_book_summary_by_currency give DVOL and options data without a key at ~20 req/s. (4) Fear & Greed: https://api.alternative.me/fng/?limit=N&format=json, no key. (5) ETF flows: Farside is HTML-only (table class="etf") with a Cloudflare challenge on some cloud hosts; no free JSON source found without a key. (6) Prediction markets: Polymarket Gamma (gamma-api.polymarket.com/events?slug=..., limit 1-500) and CLOB prices-history are key-free; Kalshi trade-api v2 market data (api.elections.kalshi.com/trade-api/v2/markets, /candlesticks with period_interval 1/60/1440) is key-free; BTC markets live under Polymarket slugs like bitcoin-up-or-down-... and Kalshi series KXBTC. Official rate-limit tiers for Kalshi and Gamma, Bybit's US reachability, Coinglass Hobbyist pricing, and alternative.me terms could not be verified.

claims.claim: Coinbase Exchange public candles: GET https://api.exchange.coinbase.com/products/BTC-USD/candles?granularity=<sec>&start=<ISO8601>&end=<ISO8601>. Allowed granularity values are 60, 300, 900, 3600, 21600, 86400 seconds (1m, 5m, 15m, 1h, 6h, 1d); maximum 300 candles per request (ccxt: 'limit = 300  # max = 300'); ccxt calls it via the unauthenticated publicGetProductsIdCandles, i.e. no API key needed. Response rows are [time, low, high, open, close, volume].

Coinbase Exchange public endpoint rate limit: 10 requests per second with a burst of 15 (per a 2024 write-up citing the official docs.cdp.coinbase.com/exchange/docs/rate-limits page, which is egress-blocked here); ccxt encodes the same 10 req/s as 'rateLimit': 100 ms.

Coinbase Advanced Trade also exposes a public, no-auth candles endpoint: GET https://api.coinbase.com/api/v3/brokerage/market/products/BTC-USD/candles?start=<unix s>&end=<unix s>&granularity=ONE_MINUTE|FIVE_MINUTE|FIFTEEN_MINUTE|THIRTY_MINUTE|ONE_HOUR|TWO_HOUR|SIX_HOUR|ONE_DAY. ccxt caps requests at 300 candles ('maxLimit = 300') and notes the Advanced API public-data limit is 10 req/s.

Kraken OHLC: GET https://api.kraken.com/0/public/OHLC?pair=XBTUSD&interval=<minutes>&since=<unix s>. Interval values: 1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 240, 1440, 10080, 21600 minutes; max 720 candles per request; no authentication (ccxt publicGetOHLC, 'limit': 720). Rows are [time, open, high, low, close, vwap, volume, count].

Kraken OHLC hard limitation (quoting the official docs text as mirrored): 'Returns up to 720 of the most recent entries (older data cannot be retrieved, regardless of the value of since)' and 'the last entry in the OHLC array is for the current, not-yet-committed timeframe'. Consequence: at 1-minute granularity Kraken only gives the last 12 hours; deep history must be collected incrementally or sourced elsewhere (Coinbase/Bitstamp support start/end paging).

Kraken public REST rate limit is roughly 1 request per second per IP (ccxt comment: '# for public: 1 req/s', citing Kraken support article 206548367); ccxt sets 'rateLimit': 1000 ms and gives the OHLC call a cost of 1.2 'because 1 triggers too many requests immediately'.

Bitstamp OHLC: GET https://www.bitstamp.net/api/v2/ohlc/btcusd/?step=<sec>&limit=<n>&start=<unix s>&end=<unix s>. step values: 60, 180, 300, 900, 1800, 3600, 7200, 14400, 21600, 43200, 86400, 259200; limit min 1, max 1000 (ccxt: 'request[limit] = min(limit, 1000)  # min 1, max 1000'); public, no key (publicGetOhlcPair).
Bitstamp API rate limit: 8000 requests per 10 minutes (ccxt comment: '8000 requests per 10 minutes = 13.33 requests per second => 75ms between requests').

Binance spot klines (official docs mirror): GET /api/v3/klines?symbol=BTCUSDT&interval=<iv>&startTime&endTime&limit; 'limit | INT | NO | Default: 500; Maximum: 1000'; request weight 2; intervals 1s, 1m, 3m, 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 2h, 4h, 6h, 8h, 12h, 1d, 3d, 1w, 1M; base endpoints https://api.binance.com, api-gcp, api1-api4.binance.com. Security type NONE (no key).

Binance geo-restriction: api.binance.com (and fapi.binance.com) answer HTTP 451 with body {"code":0,"msg":"Service unavailable from a restricted location according to 'b. Eligibility' in https://www.binance.com/en/terms..."} to US IPs, including for public/unauthenticated endpoints such as /api/v3/exchangeInfo and /fapi/v1/klines. Multiple independent projects report this.

Binance official market-data-only host: 'For APIs that only send public market data, please use the base endpoint https://data-api.binance.vision'; it serves GET /api/v3/klines, /ticker/24hr, /depth, /trades, /aggTrades, /exchangeInfo etc. and 'These URLs do not require any authentication'. WebSocket equivalent: wss://data-stream.binance.vision:443/ws/btcusdt@kline_1m.

Community reports (Aug 2026) that data-api.binance.vision is not geo-restricted and works where api.binance.com returns 451, including US-hosted CI runners: go-quote README 08/19/2026 'Uses data-api.binance.vision, which needs no API key and is not geo-restricted; api.binance.com returns 451 outside eligible regions'; synth-subnet CHANGELOG says the same for US validators. Not verified from an official Binance statement.

Binance IP rate limiting: limits are weight-based per IP (X-MBX-USED-WEIGHT headers); a 429 must be backed off; repeated violations produce an automated IP ban (HTTP 418) scaling 'from 2 minutes to 3 days'; a Retry-After header gives the seconds to wait. (The concrete REQUEST_WEIGHT per-minute cap for binance.com was not captured in the fetched text; Binance.US docs show 1200 weight/minute.)

Binance.US (US-legal alternative): base https://api.binance.us; GET /api/v3/klines with 'limit | INT | NO | Default 500; max 1000', weight 1; REQUEST_WEIGHT rate limiter of 1200 per minute; same 429/418 ban rules; public market-data endpoints need no key.

Binance USDS-M futures funding-rate history (official connector docstring): GET https://fapi.binance.com/fapi/v1/fundingRate?symbol=BTCUSDT&startTime&endTime&limit ('Default 500, max 1000', ascending order). Open-interest history: GET /futures/data/openInterestHist?symbol=BTCUSDT&period=5m|15m|30m|1h|2h|4h|6h|12h|1d&limit ('Default 30, max 500'; 'Only the data of the latest 30 days is available'). No key, but fapi.binance.com is subject to the same 451 geo-block from the US.

Bybit v5 funding-rate history (official docs mirror): GET https://api.bybit.com/v5/market/funding/history?category=linear|inverse&symbol=BTCUSDT&startTime&endTime&limit ('Limit for data size per page. [1, 200]. Default: 200'); 'Passing only startTime returns an error'; covers USDT/USDC and inverse perpetuals; public market endpoint, no auth.

Bybit v5 open interest: GET /v5/market/open-interest?category=linear|inverse&symbol=BTCUSDT&intervalTime=5min|15min|30min|1h|4h|1d&startTime&endTime&limit ('[1, 200]. Default: 50'); history back to the symbol's launch time; no auth.

Bybit v5 klines: GET /v5/market/kline?category=spot|linear|inverse&symbol=BTCUSDT&interval=1|3|5|15|30|60|120|240|360|720|D|W|M&start&end&limit ('[1, 1000]. Default: 200'); results sorted in reverse by startTime; no auth.

Bybit IP rate limit: 'No more than 600 requests are allowed in any 5-second window' for GET/POST combined, shared across api.bybit.com and api.bytick.com for spot, derivatives and options; HTTP 403 means the IP is temporarily (usually 30 min) or permanently banned.

Deribit DVOL history: GET https://www.deribit.com/api/v2/public/get_volatility_index_data?currency=BTC&start_timestamp=<ms>&end_timestamp=<ms>&resolution=<r>, where resolution is one of the strings '1', '60', '3600', '43200', '1D' (seconds, or 1D); public method, no authentication; returns candles of the volatility index for charting. ccxt lists get_volatility_index_data among public GET methods with cost 1.

Deribit rate limits (ccxt comment): '20 requests per second for non-matching-engine endpoints' (i.e. public market-data calls) and '5 requests per second for matching-engine endpoints'; ccxt uses rateLimit 50 ms. Base REST URL https://www.deribit.com, testnet https://test.deribit.com.

Other useful Deribit public (no-key) methods listed in ccxt: public/get_book_summary_by_currency?currency=BTC&kind=option (whole options surface incl. mark IV/OI, one base currency per call), public/get_instruments, public/get_funding_rate_value and public/get_funding_rate_history (BTC-PERPETUAL), public/get_historical_volatility, public/get_index_price, and public/get_tradingview_chart_data for candles with resolution 1,3,5,10,15,30,60,120,180,360,720 (minutes) or 1D.

Crypto Fear & Greed index (alternative.me): GET https://api.alternative.me/fng/?limit=<N>&format=json (optional date_format=us|kr); no API key; JSON 'data' array with value, value_classification, timestamp, time_until_update; a large limit (e.g. limit=3000) returns the full daily history. Pattern confirmed across freqtrade/ftui, richmanbtc/bot_snippets and others; the official page itself is egress-blocked here.
Fear & Greed full-history pull example: 'https://api.alternative.me/fng/?limit=3000' loaded straight into a pandas DataFrame, dropping the row with time_until_update (the current, incomplete day).

Farside spot-BTC-ETF flows (https://farside.co.uk/btc/) is a plain HTML page whose numbers sit in a <table class="etf"> (per-issuer daily flows in USD millions with a Total column); there is no JSON/CSV API, so it must be scraped (pandas.read_html / BeautifulSoup). Several open-source trackers do exactly this.

Farside is 'behind a Cloudflare bot challenge from this host and returns 403 even with browser-like UAs' from at least one cloud host; 'Other free aggregators (sosovalue, bitmex research) are similarly blocked or require keys.' Whether a residential IP on the user's PC gets through is untested.

Coinglass v4 API requires an API key on every endpoint (header 'CG-API-KEY: ${YOUR_API_KEY}', base https://open-api-v4.coinglass.com). Rate limits by plan: HOBBYIST 30 requests/min, STARTUP 80/min, STANDARD 300/min, PROFESSIONAL 1200/min; response headers API-KEY-MAX-LIMIT and API-KEY-USE-LIMIT report usage. Pricing/free-ness of the Hobbyist tier is not stated in the repo.

Coinglass JSON source for US spot-BTC-ETF flows: GET https://open-api-v4.coinglass.com/api/etf/bitcoin/flow-history (no parameters) returns daily objects with timestamp (ms), flow_usd, price_usd and an etf_flows[] breakdown by etf_ticker; marked 'Hobbyist: Available'. Related: /api/etf/bitcoin/list, /net-assets/history, /premium-discount/history, /price/history, /aum; Hong Kong flows at /api/hk-etf/bitcoin/flow-history.

Coinglass funding-rate history: GET /api/futures/funding-rate/history?exchange=Binance&symbol=BTCUSDT&interval=1m|3m|5m|15m|30m|1h|4h|6h|8h|12h|1d|1w&limit(<=1000, default 1000)&start_time&end_time (ms); OI-weighted variant /api/futures/funding-rate/oi-weight-history; both 'Hobbyist: Available'.
